title: Final Project: Architecture Integration Capstone
text:
All five modules integrated: Kafka ingestion → Bronze/Silver/Gold Lakehouse → Quality Gate → RAG serving → Orchestration DAG with lineage.

!pip install pandas chromadb sentence-transformers loguru


import osimport jsonimport uuidimport randomfrom datetime import datetime, timedeltafrom collections import defaultdictimport pandas as pdimport chromadbfrom chromadb.utils.embedding_functions import SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunctionfrom sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformerfrom loguru import loggerlogger.add("capstone_run.log", rotation="10 MB")BRONZE_PATH = "./lakehouse/bronze"SILVER_PATH = "./lakehouse/silver"GOLD_PATH   = "./lakehouse/gold"


# =====================================================================# MODULE 1 — INGESTION (Kafka simulation)


# =====================================================================class MockKafka:    """    Simulates Kafka's topic/partition/offset model.    In real Kafka:      - Topics are split into partitions (parallel ordered logs).      - Producers assign events to partitions (round-robin or key-hash).      - Consumer groups share partitions — each partition to one member.      - Offsets are committed so consumers can resume after failure.    """    def __init__(self):        self.topics  = defaultdict(list)        self.offsets = defaultdict(int)    def produce(self, topic: str, event: dict):        self.topics[topic].append({            "offset":     self.offsets[topic],            "event_time": datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),            "payload":    event,        })        self.offsets[topic] += 1    def consume_all(self, topic: str) -> list[dict]:        return self.topics.pop(topic, [])def module1_ingest(kafka: MockKafka) -> int:    """    Produces synthetic e-commerce order events to the orders_raw topic.    Replace this function with a real Kafka producer for your project.    """    logger.info("[MODULE 1] Ingestion — producing events to Kafka...")    products  = ["Laptop", "Mouse", "Keyboard", "Monitor", "Headset", "Webcam"]    countries = ["SA", "AE", "EG", "KW", "BH", "QA"]    for i in range(25):        kafka.produce("orders_raw", {            "order_id":    f"ORD-{1000 + i:04d}",            "customer_id": f"CUST-{random.randint(1, 10):03d}",            "product":     random.choice(products),            "amount":      round(random.uniform(50.0, 2000.0), 2),            "country":     random.choice(countries),            "landed_at":   datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),        })    count = kafka.offsets["orders_raw"]    logger.success(f"[MODULE 1] {count} events published to orders_raw")    return count


# =====================================================================# MODULE 2 — STORAGE (Bronze → Silver → Gold)


# =====================================================================def module2_storage(kafka: MockKafka) -> dict[str, str]:    """    Implements the Medallion Architecture (Delta Lakehouse pattern):      Bronze — Raw append: every field, no cleaning, with ingestion timestamp.               In production: Spark Structured Streaming writes directly here               using .format('delta').mode('append').      Silver — Cleansed: nulls dropped, invalid rows filtered, types enforced.               In production: a dbt model with enforced: true transforms Bronze.      Gold   — Aggregated: business-level metrics ready for BI and AI serving.               In production: scheduled Spark batch job or dbt mart model.    """    logger.info("[MODULE 2] Storage — Bronze → Silver → Gold pipeline...")    events   = kafka.consume_all("orders_raw")    payloads = [e["payload"] for e in events]    for path in [BRONZE_PATH, SILVER_PATH, GOLD_PATH]:        os.makedirs(path, exist_ok=True)    # Bronze: raw, no transformation    bronze_df   = pd.DataFrame(payloads)    bronze_file = f"{BRONZE_PATH}/orders_{int(datetime.utcnow().timestamp())}.parquet"    bronze_df.to_parquet(bronze_file, index=False)    logger.info(f"[MODULE 2] Bronze: {len(bronze_df)} rows → {bronze_file}")    # Silver: cleansed    silver_df = bronze_df.dropna()    silver_df = silver_df[silver_df["amount"] > 0].copy()    silver_df = silver_df[silver_df["country"].str.match(r"^[A-Z]{2}$", na=False)]    silver_file = f"{SILVER_PATH}/orders_clean.parquet"    silver_df.to_parquet(silver_file, index=False)    dropped = len(bronze_df) - len(silver_df)    logger.info(f"[MODULE 2] Silver: {len(silver_df)} rows ({dropped} dropped in cleansing)")    # Gold: revenue by country    gold_df = (        silver_df        .groupby("country")        .agg(            total_orders   = ("order_id", "count"),            total_revenue  = ("amount",   "sum"),            avg_order_value= ("amount",   "mean"),        )        .reset_index()        .sort_values("total_revenue", ascending=False)    )    gold_df["avg_order_value"] = gold_df["avg_order_value"].round(2)    gold_file = f"{GOLD_PATH}/revenue_by_country.parquet"    gold_df.to_parquet(gold_file, index=False)    logger.success("[MODULE 2] Gold layer ready")    return {"bronze": bronze_file, "silver": silver_file, "gold": gold_file}


# =====================================================================# MODULE 3 — QUALITY GATE (DAMA + Great Expectations-style)


# =====================================================================def module3_quality(silver_path: str) -> bool:    """    Runs DAMA quality checks on the Silver layer before serving.    Returns True if all checks pass (pipeline continues), False otherwise.    In production: replace each check with a Great Expectations expectation:      expect_column_values_to_not_be_null()      expect_column_values_to_be_between()      expect_column_values_to_be_unique()      expect_column_values_to_match_regex()    """    logger.info("[MODULE 3] Quality Gate — validating Silver layer...")    df     = pd.read_parquet(silver_path)    passed = True    checks = [        (            "Completeness",            df.isnull().sum().sum() == 0,            f"{df.isnull().sum().sum()} null values found",        ),        (            "Accuracy (amount > 0)",            (df["amount"] > 0).all(),            "Negative or zero amounts detected",        ),        (            "Uniqueness (order_id)",            df.duplicated("order_id").sum() == 0,            f"{df.duplicated('order_id').sum()} duplicate order IDs",        ),        (            "Validity (country ISO-3166)",            df["country"].str.match(r"^[A-Z]{2}$", na=False).all(),            "Non-ISO country codes detected",        ),        (            "Timeliness (landed within 10 min)",            (                pd.to_datetime(df["landed_at"])                >= datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(minutes=10)            ).all(),            "Records landed outside the 10-minute SLA",        ),    ]    for name, result, fail_detail in checks:        if result:            logger.success(f"  [PASSED] {name}")        else:            logger.warning(f"  [FAILED] {name}: {fail_detail}")            passed = False    return passed


# =====================================================================# MODULE 4 — SERVING (RAG pipeline over Gold data)


# =====================================================================def module4_rag_serve(gold_path: str):    """    Indexes Gold layer records into ChromaDB and answers analytical queries    using Retrieval-Augmented Generation.    In production:      - Use a persistent Chroma client or Pinecone for the vector index.      - Call an actual LLM API (OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic) for answers.      - Implement hybrid search (BM25 + vector) + cross-encoder reranking.    """    logger.info("[MODULE 4] Serving — building RAG index over Gold data...")    df = pd.read_parquet(gold_path)    # Convert each Gold row into a human-readable document    documents = [        (            f"Country {row.country}: {int(row.total_orders)} orders, "            f"total revenue ${row.total_revenue:.2f}, "            f"average order value ${row.avg_order_value:.2f}."        )        for _, row in df.iterrows()    ]    ef = SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")    client = chromadb.Client()    try:        client.delete_collection("capstone_gold")    except Exception:        pass    collection = client.create_collection("capstone_gold", embedding_function=ef)    collection.add(        ids       = [f"row_{i}" for i in range(len(documents))],        documents = documents,    )    queries = [        "Which country generated the most revenue?",        "What is the average order value in Saudi Arabia?",        "Which markets have the most orders?",    ]    embed_model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")    for query in queries:        results  = collection.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=2)        top_docs = results["documents"][0]        print(f"\n  🔍 RAG Query: {query}")        print(f"  📄 Retrieved: {top_docs[0]}")        print(f"  🤖 [LLM would answer here using the retrieved context]")    logger.success("[MODULE 4] RAG serving complete")


# =====================================================================# MODULE 5 — ORCHESTRATION (Airflow-style DAG)


# =====================================================================def module5_orchestrate():    """    Executes all five modules in topological (dependency) order.    In production: each function below becomes a PythonOperator in    an Airflow DAG with depends_on_past=False and retries=2.    DAG shape:      ingest → storage → quality_gate → serve (if passed)                                      → quarantine (if failed)    XCom equivalent: paths dict passes dataset locations between tasks.    Lineage events are the audit trail — one event per task transition.    """    logger.info("[MODULE 5] DAG orchestrator starting...")    run_id  = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]    lineage = []    def emit(task: str, event: str, details: dict = None):        lineage.append({            "runId":  run_id,            "task":   task,            "event":  event,            "ts":     datetime.utcnow().isoformat(),            **(details or {}),        })    kafka = MockKafka()    # Task 1: Ingest    emit("ingest", "START")    count = module1_ingest(kafka)    emit("ingest", "COMPLETE", {"events_produced": count})    # Task 2: Storage    emit("storage", "START")    paths = module2_storage(kafka)    emit("storage", "COMPLETE", paths)    # Task 3: Quality gate (branching)    emit("quality_gate", "START")    quality_ok = module3_quality(paths["silver"])    if quality_ok:        emit("quality_gate", "COMPLETE")        # Task 4: Serve (downstream task — only runs if quality passed)        emit("rag_serve", "START")        module4_rag_serve(paths["gold"])        emit("rag_serve", "COMPLETE")    else:        emit("quality_gate", "FAIL", {"action": "quarantine — serve step skipped"})        logger.error("[MODULE 5] Quality gate failed — downstream serve step skipped.")    # Write lineage audit trail    os.makedirs("lineage_events", exist_ok=True)    lineage_path = f"lineage_events/run_{run_id}.json"    with open(lineage_path, "w") as f:        json.dump(lineage, f, indent=2)    logger.info(f"[MODULE 5] Lineage → {lineage_path}")    return quality_ok


# =====================================================================# ENTRY POINT


# =====================================================================def main():    print("=" * 65)    print("  Day 5 Capstone — Architecture Integration")    print("=" * 65)    success = module5_orchestrate()    print("\n" + "=" * 65)    if success:        print("✅ All 5 modules ran successfully end-to-end.")        print("")        print("   Output directories:")        print(f"   • ./lakehouse/bronze/  — raw ingested records")        print(f"   • ./lakehouse/silver/  — cleansed, validated records")        print(f"   • ./lakehouse/gold/    — revenue aggregation by country")        print(f"   • ./lineage_events/    — pipeline audit trail (JSON)")    else:        print("⚠️  Pipeline completed but quality gate failed.")        print("   Fix the upstream data issues and re-run.")    print("=" * 65)    print("\nTeam extension checklist:")    print("  □ Replace MockKafka → real kafka-python producer/consumer")    print("  □ Replace pandas parquet writes → PySpark + Delta Lake")    print("  □ Replace manual checks → Great Expectations checkpoints")    print("  □ Replace chromadb.Client() → persistent Chroma or Pinecone")    print("  □ Wrap module5_orchestrate() tasks in an Airflow DAG")    print("  □ Add OpenLineage HTTP emitter pointing at a Marquez server")    print("  □ Record a 10-minute demo covering all five modules")




main()

# =====================================================================
# STAGE 1 — CHUNKING (sentence-level with overlap)


# =====================================================================

def chunk_documents(docs: list[dict], chunk_size: int = 2) -> list[dict]:
    """
    Splits each document into overlapping sentence chunks.
    chunk_size = 2 means each chunk contains 2 consecutive sentences.
    Overlap of 1 sentence ensures context is not lost at chunk boundaries.
    """
    all_chunks = []
    for doc in docs:
        sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", doc["text"].strip())
        for i in range(0, len(sentences), max(1, chunk_size - 1)):
            chunk_text = " ".join(sentences[i : i + chunk_size])
            if not chunk_text.strip():
                continue
            all_chunks.append({
                "id":     f"{doc['id']}_chunk_{i:03d}",
                "text":   chunk_text,
                "doc_id": doc["id"],
            })
    return all_chunks


# =====================================================================
# STAGE 2 — VECTOR INDEX (ChromaDB + SentenceTransformer bi-encoder)


# =====================================================================

def build_vector_index(chunks: list[dict]) -> chromadb.Collection:
    """
    Embeds all chunks with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and stores them in ChromaDB.
    ChromaDB uses HNSW internally — the same index type as Pinecone/Weaviate.
    """
    print("\n📦 Building ChromaDB vector index...")
    ef = SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
    client     = chromadb.Client()
    collection = client.get_or_create_collection(
        "rag_lab_knowledge_base", embedding_function=ef
    )
    collection.add(
        ids       = [c["id"]   for c in chunks],
        documents = [c["text"] for c in chunks],
        metadatas = [{"doc_id": c["doc_id"]} for c in chunks],
    )
    print(f"   ✅ {len(chunks)} chunks indexed (HNSW backend, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings)")
    return collection


# =====================================================================
# STAGE 3 — BM25 KEYWORD INDEX


# =====================================================================

class BM25Index:
    """
    Classic TF-IDF keyword search using the BM25 ranking function.
    Finds exact keyword matches that semantic search often misses
    (e.g., product names, acronyms, version numbers like 'GPT-4').
    """

    def __init__(self, chunks: list[dict]):
        tokenised  = [c["text"].lower().split() for c in chunks]
        self.bm25  = BM25Okapi(tokenised)
        self.chunks = chunks

    def search(self, query: str, top_k: int = 10) -> list[tuple[float, dict]]:
        scores = self.bm25.get_scores(query.lower().split())
        ranked = sorted(enumerate(scores), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
        return [(score, self.chunks[idx]) for idx, score in ranked[:top_k]]


# =====================================================================
# STAGE 4 — HYBRID SEARCH WITH RECIPROCAL RANK FUSION


# =====================================================================

def reciprocal_rank_fusion(
    vector_hits: list[dict],
    bm25_hits:   list[tuple[float, dict]],
    k:           int = 60,
    top_k:       int = 6,
) -> list[dict]:
    """
    RRF score = Σ 1/(k + rank_i) across both result lists.

    k=60 is the empirically optimal constant — it prevents the top-rank
    position from dominating and rewards documents that rank consistently
    across both systems. No weights to tune: RRF is parameter-free.
    """
    rrf_scores: dict[str, float] = {}
    id_to_chunk: dict[str, dict] = {}

    for rank, hit in enumerate(vector_hits):
        cid = hit["id"]
        rrf_scores[cid] = rrf_scores.get(cid, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank + 1)
        id_to_chunk[cid] = {"id": cid, "text": hit["document"]}

    for rank, (_, chunk) in enumerate(bm25_hits):
        cid = chunk["id"]
        rrf_scores[cid] = rrf_scores.get(cid, 0.0) + 1.0 / (k + rank + 1)
        id_to_chunk[cid] = chunk

    sorted_ids = sorted(rrf_scores, key=lambda x: rrf_scores[x], reverse=True)
    return [id_to_chunk[cid] for cid in sorted_ids[:top_k]]


# =====================================================================
# STAGE 5 — CROSS-ENCODER RERANKING (Stage 2 precision gate)


# =====================================================================

def rerank(
    query:       str,
    candidates:  list[dict],
    model_name:  str = "cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2",
    top_k:       int = 3,
) -> list[dict]:
    """
    Cross-encoder jointly encodes the (query, document) pair.
    This is much more accurate than cosine similarity between
    independent embeddings, because it can model the interaction
    between query tokens and document tokens directly.

    Cost: O(n) inference calls vs O(1) for bi-encoder similarity.
    Strategy: retrieve top-50 fast with bi-encoder, rerank top-50
    with cross-encoder, return top-5 to the LLM.
    """
    print(f"  🎯 Cross-encoder reranking {len(candidates)} candidates...")
    model  = CrossEncoder(model_name)
    pairs  = [(query, c["text"]) for c in candidates]
    scores = model.predict(pairs)
    ranked = sorted(zip(scores, candidates), key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)
    return [doc for _, doc in ranked[:top_k]]


# =====================================================================
# STAGE 6 — RAG PROMPT CONSTRUCTION


# =====================================================================

def build_rag_prompt(query: str, context_docs: list[dict]) -> str:
    """
    Constructs the prompt sent to the LLM.
    In production: replace the print statement with an actual API call
    (OpenAI, Anthropic, or any OpenRouter-compatible model).
    """
    context = "\n\n".join(
        f"[Source {i+1}]: {d['text']}" for i, d in enumerate(context_docs)
    )
    return (
        "You are a data engineering expert. Answer the question strictly based\n"
        "on the provided context. Do not add information not in the context.\n\n"
        f"CONTEXT:\n{context}\n\n"
        f"QUESTION: {query}\n\n"
        "ANSWER:"
    )


# =====================================================================
# STAGE 7 — EVALUATION (simplified RAGAS-style metrics)


# =====================================================================

def evaluate(
    query:          str,
    retrieved_docs: list[dict],
    embed_model:    SentenceTransformer,
    relevance_threshold: float = 0.30,
) -> dict:
    """
    Computes two simplified metrics using cosine similarity:

    Context Precision = fraction of retrieved chunks above the
                        relevance threshold (no noise in context).
    Avg Similarity    = mean cosine score between query and chunks
                        (proxy for Context Recall).

    In production: use RAGAS which calls an LLM judge for all four metrics.
    Alert if faithfulness < 0.85 — it means the LLM is hallucinating.
    """
    q_emb   = embed_model.encode(query, normalize_embeddings=True)
    scores  = [
        float(np.dot(q_emb, embed_model.encode(d["text"], normalize_embeddings=True)))
        for d in retrieved_docs
    ]
    relevant = sum(s > relevance_threshold for s in scores)
    return {
        "context_precision": round(relevant / len(scores), 3),
        "avg_similarity":    round(sum(scores) / len(scores), 3),
        "chunks_in_context": len(retrieved_docs),
    }

        for i, doc in enumerate(final_docs, 1):
            print(f"    [{i}] {doc['text'][:110]}...")

        print("\n  📋 Prompt sent to LLM (first 300 chars):")
        print(f"    {prompt[:300]}...")
        print("\n  [In production: call your LLM API here with the full prompt]")

        # Evaluate
        metrics = evaluate(query, final_docs, embed_model)
        print(f"\n  📊 Retrieval metrics: {metrics}")
        if metrics["context_precision"] < 0.5:
            print("  ⚠️  Low precision — consider increasing ef or lowering chunk overlap")
        else:
            print("  ✅  Retrieval quality looks good")

    print("\n" + "=" * 65)
    print("Lab complete. Key takeaways:")
    print("  1. Vector search finds semantic matches — misses exact terms")
    print("  2. BM25 finds exact keyword matches — misses paraphrases")
    print("  3. RRF fuses both result lists without needing to tune weights")
    print("  4. Cross-encoder adds a high-precision second stage (at O(n) cost)")
    print("  5. Always measure: context precision, recall, faithfulness, relevance")
    print("=" * 65)


# =====================================================================
# STAGE 8 — PERSISTENCE & METADATA FILTERING (the DATABASE half of “vector database”)


# =====================================================================

def demo_persistence_and_filtering(chunks: list[dict]) -> None:
    """
    Stage 2 used chromadb.Client() - in-memory, gone the moment the process
    exits. A real vector DATABASE has to survive a restart, and it has to
    support narrowing a search by metadata, not similarity alone. Neither
    is shown anywhere above, so this stage shows both, for real:

    1. Write to a PersistentClient, drop the handle (simulating the process
       exiting), reopen a fresh client pointed at the same path, and confirm
       the chunks are still there with no re-embedding.
    2. Run the same query with and without a `where={"doc_id": ...}` filter,
       and show the candidate set actually narrows to just that document.
    """
    import shutil
    from pathlib import Path

    persist_dir = Path("chroma_persist_demo")
    shutil.rmtree(persist_dir, ignore_errors=True)
    ef = SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

    print("\n\U0001F4be Writing to a PersistentClient (not the in-memory Client from Stage 2)...")
    client1 = chromadb.PersistentClient(path=str(persist_dir))
    coll1 = client1.get_or_create_collection("persist_demo", embedding_function=ef)
    coll1.add(
        ids       = [c["id"]   for c in chunks],
        documents = [c["text"] for c in chunks],
        metadatas = [{"doc_id": c["doc_id"]} for c in chunks],
    )
    print(f"   wrote {coll1.count()} chunks to disk at {persist_dir}/")
    del client1, coll1   # the closest a notebook gets to "the process exited"

    client2 = chromadb.PersistentClient(path=str(persist_dir))
    coll2 = client2.get_or_create_collection("persist_demo", embedding_function=ef)
    print(f"   reopened from disk, zero re-embedding calls: {coll2.count()} chunks still there")

    query = "How does indexing work?"
    unfiltered = coll2.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=8)
    filtered = coll2.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=8, where={"doc_id": "doc_004"})
    unf_docs = sorted(set(m["doc_id"] for m in unfiltered["metadatas"][0]))
    filt_docs = sorted(set(m["doc_id"] for m in filtered["metadatas"][0]))

    print(f"\n   unfiltered query \u2192 {len(unfiltered['ids'][0])} candidates, from doc_ids {unf_docs}")
    print(f"   where=doc_004 only \u2192 {len(filtered['ids'][0])} candidates, from doc_ids {filt_docs}")
    print("   same similarity ranking underneath - metadata filtering narrows the")
    print("   candidate pool BEFORE ranking, which is what a real multi-tenant or")
    print("   access-controlled RAG system needs (e.g. where={\"customer_id\": ...}).")

    # Release both PersistentClient handles before deleting the directory -
    # SQLite (what Chroma persists to) holds the file open until every
    # reference is gone, and Windows (unlike POSIX) refuses to remove a file
    # that's still locked. Skipping this leaves chroma_persist_demo/ on disk
    # every single run - found by actually running this cell, not by reading it.
    del client2, coll2
    import gc
    gc.collect()
    shutil.rmtree(persist_dir, ignore_errors=True)

title: Lab: Real-Time Streaming Pipeline with Kafka & Delta Lake
text:
This single notebook covers everything in today’s lab:

Mock Kafka streaming pipeline — producers, a stateful window processor (tumbling/sliding/watermark), and a Delta Lake ACID sink.
Real Kafka round trip — one real kafka-python producer/consumer exchange with a Pydantic schema gate, run against a real local broker.


!pip install pyspark==3.5.0 delta-spark==3.2.0

Requirement already satisfied: pyspark==4.0.1 in /usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages (4.0.1)
Requirement already satisfied: delta-spark==4.3.0 in /usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages (4.3.0)
Requirement already satisfied: py4j==0.10.9.9 in /usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages (from pyspark==4.0.1) (0.10.9.9)
Requirement already satisfied: importlib_metadata<=8.7.1,>=1.0.0 in /usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages (from delta-spark==4.3.0) (8.7.1)
Requirement already satisfied: zipp>=3.20 in /usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages (from importlib_metadata<=8.7.1,>=1.0.0->delta-spark==4.3.0) (4.1.0)





import asyncio
import os
import random
import shutil
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from collections import defaultdict
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.types import (
    StructType, StructField, StringType, DoubleType, IntegerType
)
from delta import configure_spark_with_delta_pip


# =====================================================================
# 1. BACKBONE — Mock Kafka Broker (partitions + offsets)


# =====================================================================

class MockKafkaBroker:
    """
    Simulates Apache Kafka's core model.

    In real Kafka:
      - A topic is split into N partitions (ordered, immutable logs).
      - Each message gets an offset — its address within the partition.
      - A consumer group shares partitions; each partition goes to
        exactly one member, so adding consumers beyond the partition
        count yields no extra throughput.
      - Committed offsets let consumers resume after a crash.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.topics  = defaultdict(asyncio.Queue)
        self.offsets = defaultdict(int)

    async def publish(self, topic: str, message: dict):
        offset = self.offsets[topic]
        self.offsets[topic] += 1
        await self.topics[topic].put({
            "offset":     offset,
            "event_time": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
            "topic":      topic,
            "payload":    message,
        })

    async def consume(self, topic: str) -> dict:
        return await self.topics[topic].get()


def init_delta_spark() -> SparkSession:
    builder = (
        SparkSession.builder
        .appName("Day2_RealTimeStreamingPipeline")
        .master("local[*]")
        .config("spark.sql.extensions",
                "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
        .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
        .config("spark.sql.warehouse.dir", "./data/warehouse")
    )
    spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(builder).getOrCreate()
    spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")
    return spark


# =====================================================================
# 2. INGESTION LAYER — Three concurrent IoT producers


# =====================================================================

async def machine_producer(broker: MockKafkaBroker, machine_id: str):
    """
    Simulates a factory sensor streaming temperature readings every 300ms.
    12% chance of a spike anomaly to trigger downstream alerts.
    """
    print(f"  🏭 [PRODUCER] {machine_id} stream online.")
    while True:
        is_spike = random.random() < 0.12
        temp = random.uniform(92.0, 118.0) if is_spike else random.uniform(58.0, 78.0)
        await broker.publish("factory_sensors_raw", {
            "machine_id": machine_id,
            "temperature": round(temp, 2),
            "event_ts":   datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        })
        await asyncio.sleep(0.3)


# =====================================================================
# 3. COMPUTE LAYER — Stream processor with window types + watermark


# =====================================================================

class StreamProcessor:
    """
    Stateful stream processing engine — mirrors Flink / Spark Structured Streaming.

    Three window types demonstrated:
      TUMBLING   — fixed, non-overlapping 1-second buckets.
                   Every event belongs to exactly one bucket.
                   Use case: per-second event count, hourly totals.

      SLIDING    — overlapping rolling window over the last 3 seconds.
                   The same event can appear in multiple windows.
                   Use case: rolling average temperature or CPU.

      WATERMARK  — events older than WATERMARK_S seconds are dropped.
                   This bounds state memory and lets the engine close
                   windows cleanly. Larger watermark = more completeness
                   but higher latency.
    """

    WATERMARK_S      = 2
    SLIDING_WINDOW_S = 3

    def __init__(self, broker: MockKafkaBroker, threshold: float):
        self.broker    = broker
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.sliding   = defaultdict(list)
        self.tumbling  = defaultdict(list)
        self.watermark = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    async def run(self):
        print(f"  🧠 [PROCESSOR] Window engine live. Threshold: {self.threshold}°C")
        while True:
            event   = await self.broker.consume("factory_sensors_raw")
            payload = event["payload"]
            m_id    = payload["machine_id"]
            val     = payload["temperature"]
            now     = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

            # Watermark — drop late events
            if now < self.watermark - timedelta(seconds=self.WATERMARK_S):
                print(f"  ⚠️  [WATERMARK] Late event from {m_id} dropped.")
                continue
            self.watermark = max(self.watermark, now)

            # Sliding window — rolling average
            self.sliding[m_id].append((now, val))
            cutoff = now - timedelta(seconds=self.SLIDING_WINDOW_S)
            self.sliding[m_id] = [
                (t, v) for t, v in self.sliding[m_id] if t > cutoff
            ]
            rolling_avg = (
                sum(v for _, v in self.sliding[m_id]) / len(self.sliding[m_id])
            )

            # Tumbling window — count events in this 1-second bucket
            bucket = now.strftime("%H:%M:%S")
            self.tumbling[bucket].append(val)
            bucket_count = len(self.tumbling[bucket])

            # Threshold check
            if val > self.threshold:
                await self.broker.publish("anomalies_sink", {
                    "machine_id":   m_id,
                    "value":        val,
                    "rolling_avg":  round(rolling_avg, 2),
                    "bucket":       bucket,
                    "bucket_count": bucket_count,
                    "status":       "CRITICAL",
                })


# =====================================================================
# 4. STORAGE SINK — ACID append to Delta Lake


# =====================================================================

async def delta_sink(
    broker: MockKafkaBroker,
    spark: SparkSession,
    delta_path: str,
):
    """
    Reads anomaly alerts and commits them to Delta Lake.
    Delta's transaction log guarantees ACID — no partial writes,
    no corruption even if two writers race on the same files.
    """
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("event_time",   StringType(),  True),
        StructField("machine_id",   StringType(),  True),
        StructField("value",        DoubleType(),  True),
        StructField("rolling_avg",  DoubleType(),  True),
        StructField("bucket",       StringType(),  True),
        StructField("bucket_count", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("status",       StringType(),  True),
    ])
    print("  💾 [SINK] Delta Lake writer active.")
    while True:
        alert = await broker.consume("anomalies_sink")
        p = alert["payload"]
        row = [(
            alert["event_time"],
            p["machine_id"],
            p["value"],
            p["rolling_avg"],
            p["bucket"],
            p["bucket_count"],
            p["status"],
        )]
        spark.createDataFrame(row, schema).write \
             .format("delta").mode("append").save(delta_path)

              f"{p['value']}°C | rolling avg {p['rolling_avg']}°C | "
              f"bucket {p['bucket']} ({p['bucket_count']} events)")


# =====================================================================
# 5. PIPELINE ORCHESTRATION


# =====================================================================

async def main():
    delta_path = "./data/delta/anomalies"

    if os.path.exists("./data"):
        shutil.rmtree("./data")

    broker = MockKafkaBroker()
    spark  = init_delta_spark()

    print("\n🚀 Real-Time Streaming Pipeline booting...\n")

    processor = asyncio.create_task(
        StreamProcessor(broker, threshold=85.0).run()
    )
    sink = asyncio.create_task(
        delta_sink(broker, spark, delta_path)
    )
    producers = [

        asyncio.create_task(machine_producer(broker, "ROBOTIC_ARM_02")),
        asyncio.create_task(machine_producer(broker, "ASSEMBLY_LINE_03")),
    ]

    print("  Streaming for 8 seconds...\n")
    await asyncio.sleep(8.0)

    for task in [processor, sink, *producers]:

    print("\n📊 Final Delta Lake state (all committed anomalies):")

import json
import time

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError, field_validator

TOPIC = "factory_sensors_raw"
BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS = "localhost:9092"


class SensorReading(BaseModel):
    """Same shape the mock pipeline's producers emit — reused here as the schema gate."""

    machine_id: str
    temperature: float
    event_ts: str

    @field_validator("temperature")
    @classmethod
    def plausible_range(cls, v: float) -> float:
        if not (-40.0 <= v <= 200.0):
            raise ValueError(f"temperature {v} outside plausible sensor range")
        return v


def produce_sample_messages():
    from kafka import KafkaProducer

    producer = KafkaProducer(
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
        value_serializer=lambda v: json.dumps(v).encode("utf-8"),
    )

    good = [
        {"machine_id": "CNC_MILL_01", "temperature": 71.4, "event_ts": "2026-06-29T10:00:00Z"},
        {"machine_id": "ROBOTIC_ARM_02", "temperature": 68.9, "event_ts": "2026-06-29T10:00:01Z"},
    ]
    # A malformed message on purpose, to prove the consumer's schema gate catches it
    # instead of crashing the pipeline.
    bad = {"machine_id": "ASSEMBLY_LINE_03", "temperature": "not_a_number", "event_ts": "2026-06-29T10:00:02Z"}

    for msg in good + [bad]:
        producer.send(TOPIC, msg)
        print(f"  [PRODUCER] sent -> {msg}")
    producer.flush()
    producer.close()


def consume_and_validate(max_messages: int = 3, timeout_s: int = 10):
    from kafka import KafkaConsumer

    consumer = KafkaConsumer(
        TOPIC,
        bootstrap_servers=BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS,
        auto_offset_reset="earliest",
        enable_auto_commit=True,
        group_id="day2-schema-check",
        value_deserializer=lambda v: json.loads(v.decode("utf-8")),
        consumer_timeout_ms=timeout_s * 1000,
    )

    accepted, rejected = 0, 0
    for record in consumer:
        try:
            reading = SensorReading.model_validate(record.value)
            accepted += 1
            print(f"  [CONSUMER] accepted @offset {record.offset}: {reading}")
        except ValidationError as e:
            rejected += 1
            print(f"  [CONSUMER] REJECTED @offset {record.offset}: {e.errors()[0]['msg']}")
        if accepted + rejected >= max_messages:
            break
    consumer.close()
    print(f"\n  Summary: {accepted} accepted, {rejected} rejected by the schema gate.")


def main():
    print("Real Kafka round trip (topic: {})".format(TOPIC))
    try:
        produce_sample_messages()
        time.sleep(1)
        consume_and_validate()
    except ImportError as e:
        print(f"\nMissing dependency: {e}")
        print("Install it first: pip install -r requirements.txt")

import asyncio
import os
import random
import shutil
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from collections import defaultdict
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.types import (
    StructType, StructField, StringType, DoubleType, IntegerType
)
from delta import configure_spark_with_delta_pip


# =====================================================================
# 1. BACKBONE — Mock Kafka Broker (partitions + offsets)


# =====================================================================

class MockKafkaBroker:
    """
    Simulates Apache Kafka's core model.

    In real Kafka:
      - A topic is split into N partitions (ordered, immutable logs).
      - Each message gets an offset — its address within the partition.
      - A consumer group shares partitions; each partition goes to
        exactly one member, so adding consumers beyond the partition
        count yields no extra throughput.
      - Committed offsets let consumers resume after a crash.
    """

    def __init__(self):
        self.topics  = defaultdict(asyncio.Queue)
        self.offsets = defaultdict(int)

    async def publish(self, topic: str, message: dict):
        offset = self.offsets[topic]
        self.offsets[topic] += 1
        await self.topics[topic].put({
            "offset":     offset,
            "event_time": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
            "topic":      topic,
            "payload":    message,
        })

    async def consume(self, topic: str) -> dict:
        return await self.topics[topic].get()


def init_delta_spark() -> SparkSession:
    builder = (
        SparkSession.builder
        .appName("Day2_RealTimeStreamingPipeline")
        .master("local[*]")
        .config("spark.sql.extensions",
                "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
        .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
        .config("spark.sql.warehouse.dir", "./data/warehouse")
    )
    spark = configure_spark_with_delta_pip(builder).getOrCreate()
    spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")
    return spark


# =====================================================================
# 2. INGESTION LAYER — Three concurrent IoT producers


# =====================================================================

async def machine_producer(broker: MockKafkaBroker, machine_id: str):
    """
    Simulates a factory sensor streaming temperature readings every 300ms.
    12% chance of a spike anomaly to trigger downstream alerts.
    """
    print(f"  🏭 [PRODUCER] {machine_id} stream online.")
    while True:
        is_spike = random.random() < 0.12
        temp = random.uniform(92.0, 118.0) if is_spike else random.uniform(58.0, 78.0)
        await broker.publish("factory_sensors_raw", {
            "machine_id": machine_id,
            "temperature": round(temp, 2),
            "event_ts":   datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        })
        await asyncio.sleep(0.3)


# =====================================================================
# 3. COMPUTE LAYER — Stream processor with window types + watermark


# =====================================================================

class StreamProcessor:
    """
    Stateful stream processing engine — mirrors Flink / Spark Structured Streaming.

    Three window types demonstrated:
      TUMBLING   — fixed, non-overlapping 1-second buckets.
                   Every event belongs to exactly one bucket.
                   Use case: per-second event count, hourly totals.

      SLIDING    — overlapping rolling window over the last 3 seconds.
                   The same event can appear in multiple windows.
                   Use case: rolling average temperature or CPU.

      WATERMARK  — events older than WATERMARK_S seconds are dropped.
                   This bounds state memory and lets the engine close
                   windows cleanly. Larger watermark = more completeness
                   but higher latency.
    """

    WATERMARK_S      = 2
    SLIDING_WINDOW_S = 3

    def __init__(self, broker: MockKafkaBroker, threshold: float):
        self.broker    = broker
        self.threshold = threshold
        self.sliding   = defaultdict(list)
        self.tumbling  = defaultdict(list)
        self.watermark = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

    async def run(self):
        print(f"  🧠 [PROCESSOR] Window engine live. Threshold: {self.threshold}°C")
        while True:
            event   = await self.broker.consume("factory_sensors_raw")
            payload = event["payload"]
            m_id    = payload["machine_id"]
            val     = payload["temperature"]
            now     = datetime.now(timezone.utc)

            # Watermark — drop late events
            if now < self.watermark - timedelta(seconds=self.WATERMARK_S):
                print(f"  ⚠️  [WATERMARK] Late event from {m_id} dropped.")
                continue
            self.watermark = max(self.watermark, now)

            # Sliding window — rolling average
            self.sliding[m_id].append((now, val))
            cutoff = now - timedelta(seconds=self.SLIDING_WINDOW_S)
            self.sliding[m_id] = [
                (t, v) for t, v in self.sliding[m_id] if t > cutoff
            ]
            rolling_avg = (
                sum(v for _, v in self.sliding[m_id]) / len(self.sliding[m_id])
            )

            # Tumbling window — count events in this 1-second bucket
            bucket = now.strftime("%H:%M:%S")
            self.tumbling[bucket].append(val)
            bucket_count = len(self.tumbling[bucket])

            # Threshold check
            if val > self.threshold:
                await self.broker.publish("anomalies_sink", {
                    "machine_id":   m_id,
                    "value":        val,
                    "rolling_avg":  round(rolling_avg, 2),
                    "bucket":       bucket,
                    "bucket_count": bucket_count,
                    "status":       "CRITICAL",
                })


# =====================================================================
# 4. STORAGE SINK — ACID append to Delta Lake


# =====================================================================

async def delta_sink(
    broker: MockKafkaBroker,
    spark: SparkSession,
    delta_path: str,
):
    """
    Reads anomaly alerts and commits them to Delta Lake.
    Delta's transaction log guarantees ACID — no partial writes,
    no corruption even if two writers race on the same files.
    """
    schema = StructType([
        StructField("event_time",   StringType(),  True),
        StructField("machine_id",   StringType(),  True),
        StructField("value",        DoubleType(),  True),
        StructField("rolling_avg",  DoubleType(),  True),
        StructField("bucket",       StringType(),  True),
        StructField("bucket_count", IntegerType(), True),
        StructField("status",       StringType(),  True),
    ])
    print("  💾 [SINK] Delta Lake writer active.")
    while True:
        alert = await broker.consume("anomalies_sink")
        p = alert["payload"]
        row = [(
            alert["event_time"],
            p["machine_id"],
            p["value"],
            p["rolling_avg"],
            p["bucket"],
            p["bucket_count"],
            p["status"],
        )]
        spark.createDataFrame(row, schema).write \
             .format("delta").mode("append").save(delta_path)
        print(f"  🚨 [DELTA WRITE] {p['machine_id']} — "
              f"{p['value']}°C | rolling avg {p['rolling_avg']}°C | "
              f"bucket {p['bucket']} ({p['bucket_count']} events)")


# =====================================================================
# 5. PIPELINE ORCHESTRATION


# =====================================================================

async def main():
    delta_path = "./data/delta/anomalies"

    if os.path.exists("./data"):
        shutil.rmtree("./data")

    broker = MockKafkaBroker()
    spark  = init_delta_spark()

    print("\n🚀 Real-Time Streaming Pipeline booting...\n")

    processor = asyncio.create_task(
        StreamProcessor(broker, threshold=85.0).run()
    )
    sink = asyncio.create_task(
        delta_sink(broker, spark, delta_path)
    )
    producers = [
        asyncio.create_task(machine_producer(broker, "CNC_MILL_01")),
        asyncio.create_task(machine_producer(broker, "ROBOTIC_ARM_02")),
        asyncio.create_task(machine_producer(broker, "ASSEMBLY_LINE_03")),
    ]

    print("  Streaming for 8 seconds...\n")
    await asyncio.sleep(8.0)

    for task in [processor, sink, *producers]:
        task.cancel()

    print("\n📊 Final Delta Lake state (all committed anomalies):")
    if os.path.exists(delta_path):
        spark.read.format("delta").load(delta_path) \
             .orderBy("event_time").show(truncate=False)
    else:
        print("  No anomalies recorded in this run — lower the threshold to see more.")

    spark.stop()
    print("\n🏁 Pipeline shut down cleanly.")

title: Modern Data Engineering for AI Systems
text:

The architectural insight isn’t any single box — it’s the order and the gating. Data quality sits before governance, and governance sits before storage, because a system that governs or stores bad data has already failed; catching it earlier is strictly cheaper. RAG serving sits at the very end, downstream of everything else, because a RAG answer is only as trustworthy as the governed, quality-checked data it was indexed from — this is the direct, practical answer to Day 3’s question of why RAG systems hallucinate: they retrieve from whatever they were given, so if the retrieval corpus was never quality-gated, the model will confidently ground its answer in garbage.

title: The Unified Architecture
section: How the components work together, step by step
text:
How the components work together, step by step
Walking the diagram top to bottom as a single request’s journey:
Step 1 — Data ingestion. Real-time pipelines collect events from APIs, IoT devices, operational databases (via CDC), documents, and other enterprise systems, and land them on a topic — this is Day 2’s Kafka producer/consumer model.
Step 2 — Data quality validation. Automated checks validate schema correctness, missing fields, duplicate records, and invalid values before anything is allowed further downstream. Bad data is blocked here, not discovered later in a dashboard — this is Day 4’s quality gate.
Step 3 — Governance enforcement. Governance systems apply access policies, enforce security boundaries, track lineage, and monitor compliance. This is also Day 4, and it’s why lineage exists: a governance rule with no lineage trail can’t tell you what a policy change will actually affect.
Step 4 — Data storage. Validated, governed data lands in persistent storage — a data lake, a lakehouse, or a warehouse, depending on the platform. This course’s stack is the lakehouse: bronze (raw), silver (cleansed), gold (aggregated) — using the Delta Lake ACID guarantees, MERGE, and schema enforcement from Day 1.
Step 5 — Embedding generation. Documents and records are converted into vector embeddings using an embedding model (Day 3’s sentence-transformers or equivalent).
Step 6 — Vector storage. Those embeddings are persisted in a vector database (Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate) for similarity search.
Step 7 — RAG retrieval. AI systems retrieve the relevant enterprise knowledge semantically, rather than relying on keyword search alone.
Step 8 — AI response generation. An LLM generates a response grounded in the retrieved context — the payoff of every layer beneath it having done its job correctly.

title: The Unified Architecture
text:
Orchestrating the platform
None of the layers above wire themselves together. AI infrastructure orchestration is the automated coordination of compute, storage, networking, and AI services so the pipeline above runs reliably, efficiently, and at scale.
The simplest way to picture it: if your AI platform is an orchestra, orchestration is the conductor — making sure each section (violins, brass, percussion) plays at the right time, at the right volume, without crashing into each other. Put another way: data platforms prepare the facts, LLMs act as the brain, and orchestration is the conductor of that orchestra — it coordinates the underlying compute chips, schedules deep learning workloads, manages model deployment routes, and optimizes hardware efficiency across complex multi-cloud ecosystems. Concretely, that’s the conductor making sure ingestion, quality gating, storage, embedding, and serving each run at the right time without stepping on each other.

Workflow orchestration: the DAG
The tool most directly relevant to this week’s labs is Apache Airflow, which models a pipeline as a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) — tasks as nodes, dependencies as edges, executed in topological order:

Operators are the task types: PythonOperator, BashOperator, SparkSubmitOperator, S3KeySensor, HttpSensor.
Key configuration: schedule_interval (cron expression), start_date, retries, retry_delay, catchup=False (don’t backfill every missed run since start_date).
XCom is a lightweight key-value store for passing data between tasks — keep it small (row counts, file paths, IDs), never whole DataFrames.
BranchPythonOperator returns the task_id to run next, enabling conditional pipeline paths — exactly the “if quality gate fails, quarantine instead of serving” branch the capstone’s Module 5 already models.
Best practice: one DAG per pipeline, idempotent tasks (safe to re-run without duplicating side effects), and a sensor for every external dependency instead of a fixed sleep/wait.



Platform architecture: five integrated modules
At production scale, the reference architecture above maps onto five concrete modules wired together by that DAG, plus an observability layer running alongside all of them:

Module 1 — Ingestion: Kafka topics receive events from every source — APIs, IoT, and CDC (change data capture) from Postgres.
Module 2 — Storage: Delta Lake on S3/ADLS, split into raw (bronze), cleaned (silver), and aggregated (gold) zones.
Module 3 — Processing: Spark Structured Streaming handles the real-time path; Spark batch jobs or dbt handle the silver→gold transformation.
Module 4 — Serving: a FastAPI service reads the gold Delta tables and queries Chroma or Pinecone for vector similarity.
Module 5 — Orchestration: the Airflow DAG wires the whole pipeline together — ingest → process → validate → serve.
Observability: OpenLineage events emitted at each stage feed Marquez for lineage tracking, while Great Expectations enforces the quality gates along the way.



Beyond workflows: the other orchestration layers
At real enterprise scale, “orchestration” splits into more than just DAG scheduling. This is background context for how the tools you used this week get operated in production — not something the capstone requires you to stand up:








Orchestration layer
Manages

vLLM, Triton, BentoML, Ray Serve


Vector DB

Coordinated with the data lake’s own backup schedule


Data

Kafka, dbt, Great Expectations, dlt


Storage

CSI, Velero



Without this coordination, the failure modes are concrete: a GPU training job starves a vector DB of latency budget, an embedding job starts before its upstream chunks are ready, scaling requires slow manual provisioning, one pipeline failure takes down the whole system instead of retrying in isolation, noisy-neighbor workloads step on each other without any tenant isolation, and a version upgrade breaks consumers mid-pipeline instead of rolling out as a canary. Why AI infrastructure orchestration isn’t just DevOps with a new name
Managing an AI architecture means discarding some traditional DevOps assumptions outright, not just adding a few extra tools:








Architectural metric
Traditional software orchestration
AI infrastructure orchestration




Primary resource tracked
CPU core count and RAM utilization
GPU/TPU VRAM, High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM), and interconnect speed (NVLink)


Scaling trigger
Web traffic or API request spikes
Context size, token generation speed, batch sizes


Data dependencies
Static application code packages loaded from standard storage
Multi-gigabyte model weight tensors and dynamic vector-embedding caches



The underlying reason: a traditional web service scales by adding identical, stateless replicas — more RAM and CPU cores solve most problems. An LLM-serving or embedding workload is neither identical nor stateless in the same sense — a single model’s weights can be tens of gigabytes, live entirely in GPU memory, and its actual throughput is bound by how fast tokens stream out, not by how many requests are queued. Orchestration tools built for the first world (classic Kubernetes autoscaling on CPU%) don’t know how to reason about the second — which is exactly why the GPU/model-aware tools in the table above (Kueue, Karpenter, vLLM, Ray Serve) exist as a separate layer rather than just “more Kubernetes.”
Put simply, AI infrastructure orchestration bridges raw hardware processing power with software execution — it turns a fragmented collection of bare-metal servers and cloud instances into an automated, responsive environment that scales workloads smoothly, manages model memory footprints, and keeps AI applications running cost-effectively in production. In short, it automates the deployment, scaling, coordination, and management of AI systems, data pipelines, compute resources, and machine learning workflows across the modern enterprise.

title: The Unified Architecture
text:
Why integration is the point
A fully integrated platform is what moves an enterprise from an AI prototype to production: real-time streaming, governance compliance, automated data validation, and semantic RAG search working as one system instead of four disconnected demos. That combination is what delivers fast, safe, and reliable AI applications at scale — better AI accuracy because the RAG layer only ever sees governed, quality-checked data; fewer hallucinations because responses are grounded in a trusted corpus, not whatever happened to be lying around; and governance and compliance enforced automatically instead of depending on someone remembering a policy.
Named out as a checklist, the enterprise benefits of that combination are:

Unified AI ecosystem — all data and AI operations live inside one platform instead of four disconnected demos.
Real-time intelligence — the organization can react instantly to live events instead of waiting on a batch refresh.
Better AI accuracy — high-quality, governed data improves RAG outputs.
Reduced hallucinations — RAG grounds AI responses in trusted enterprise data instead of an ungoverned corpus.
Scalability — modern architectures scale to petabytes of data without a redesign.
Governance and compliance — security and compliance are enforced automatically, not left to someone remembering a policy.

The final project is where you build exactly this, end to end, for a real (if intentionally small) dataset.

title: Lineage and Data Observability
text: Data observability and monitoring is the practice of continuously tracking, analyzing, and validating data systems so that data stays healthy, reliable, accurate, and available — the goal is to catch data problems early enough to fix them before they affect business operations or an AI system downstream, not after. In practice that discipline chases five concrete goals: detect data failures, improve data reliability, keep pipelines under continuous monitoring, ensure data quality, and prevent broken dashboards and AI errors from ever reaching a stakeholder.
crumbs: Day 4 — Data Quality, Governance, and Lineage

title: Lineage and Data Observability
section: Monitoring tells you something broke; observability tells you why
text:
Monitoring tells you something broke; observability tells you why
In the early days of data architecture, engineers relied on basic software monitoring: write a strict rule (“alert me if the server crashes, or if the ETL job throws a 500”). That works for infrastructure failures. But as data systems grew into massive streaming pipelines feeding live AI models and executive dashboards, a new failure mode appeared: silent data corruption — the pipeline runs perfectly, no code crashes, and the data inside it is simply wrong.

Data monitoring (the “what”) is reactive and rule-based. It checks infrastructure for known errors: is the database online? Did the Airflow DAG complete? Is latency under 200ms? It tells you when something broke.
Data observability (the “why”) is proactive and inferred. It analyzes the actual data flowing through the system to detect “unknown unknowns”: why did average purchase value suddenly drop 90% today? It helps you trace the root cause of an anomaly monitoring alone would never have flagged.
crumbs: Day 4 — Data Quality, Governance, and Lineage

title: Lineage and Data Observability
section: The five pillars of data observability
text:
The five pillars of data observability
A production-grade observability system (Monte Carlo, Acceldata, Databricks) continuously evaluates data health across five dimensions. The first four are what you’d expect to check; the fifth — lineage — is different in kind: it’s the map that gives the other four their context.





graph TD
    L["Lineage — the end-to-end map"] --> F["Freshness"]
    L --> V["Volume"]
    L --> S["Schema"]
    L --> D["Distribution"]






1. Freshness (SLA timeliness). Is the data up to date? If a dashboard expects sales updates every 15 minutes but the underlying table hasn’t refreshed in 4 hours, the observability engine fires a freshness alert before an executive notices a stagnant chart.
2. Volume (completeness check). Is the scale of incoming data normal? If an ingestion pipeline usually sees ~50,000 events/hour and a batch arrives with only 2,000 — or spikes to 500,000 — that’s flagged as a critical anomaly, usually pointing to an upstream API drop or a duplicate load.
3. Schema (structural changes). Schema drift is the single biggest killer of production applications and RAG systems. If user_id gets renamed to customer_uuid, or a field’s type silently changes from integer to string, every downstream transformation can break instantly. Observability tools continuously diff schemas and alert the moment structure changes.
4. Distribution (field-level health). This looks at the statistical profile of values inside a table — mean, median, standard deviation, null-rate. If customer_age normally has a 1% null rate and an upstream change suddenly pushes 75% of rows to NULL, the pipeline didn’t crash, but the data flowing through it is completely broken.
5. Lineage (the map of dependencies). Lineage is the foundational layer that gives the other four pillars context: it builds an end-to-end trace of where data originates, how it transforms, and which dashboards or models consume it. Without it, freshness/volume/schema/distribution alerts tell you something is wrong upstream but not what downstream actually depends on the broken table.
Common tooling in this space includes Monte Carlo, Datadog, Splunk, Microsoft Fabric Monitoring, and IBM’s observability suite — all built around some combination of these five pillars.
crumbs: Day 4 — Data Quality, Governance, and Lineage

title: Lineage and Data Observability
text:
OpenLineage — lineage as structured events
OpenLineage is an open, vendor-neutral standard (a JSON schema published on GitHub) for emitting lineage as discrete events rather than a hand-maintained diagram.

Event types — START when a pipeline run begins, COMPLETE on success (with output stats), FAIL on error (with the cause).
Payload shape — run (a UUID plus facets), job (namespace + name), inputs (datasets read), outputs (datasets written).
Marquez is the reference open-source lineage server: it receives these events, stores the resulting graph, and exposes it via a REST API and UI. A pipeline can also just write the events to a local file — no server required — which is what today’s lab does.

The integration pattern is deliberately minimal: emit START before the first read, COMPLETE after the final write, and FAIL inside the except block. No changes to the pipeline’s actual transformation logic are needed. The payoff is impact analysis — the lineage graph shows every downstream job that reads a given dataset, which is exactly what you need before approving a risky schema change.
# Minimal shape of an OpenLineage RunEvent
{
  "eventType": "COMPLETE",
  "eventTime": "2026-07-31T12:00:00Z",
  "run":    {"runId": "…uuid…"},
  "job":    {"namespace": "retail_pipeline", "name": "quality_gate"},
  "inputs":  [{"namespace": "kaggle", "name": "online_retail_raw.csv"}],
  "outputs": [{"namespace": "warehouse", "name": "online_retail_clean"}]
}

title: Lineage and Data Observability
section: Lab: automated data quality gates on real e-commerce data
text:
Lab: automated data quality gates on real e-commerce data
The Day 4 lab notebook builds a full quality-gate pipeline against the UCI Online Retail Dataset — 541,909 real transactions from a UK-based online retailer (2010–2011), pulled live from Kaggle. Nothing here is synthetic or planted: roughly 25% of CustomerIDs are genuinely missing, cancelled orders carry negative quantities, and formatting is inconsistent — exactly the kind of mess a real ingestion boundary has to handle.
The notebook walks through the whole chain from today’s lesson, in order:

Download and profile the raw CSV, surfacing quality problems before any rule is written.
Enforce a RetailTransactionContract (Pydantic v2) at the pipeline boundary — rows with a missing customer ID, non-positive quantity, or malformed invoice number are rejected immediately.
Run a hand-rolled DataQualityEngine implementing all six DAMA dimensions against the contract-validated rows.
Run the same core checks again through a real Great Expectations 1.x checkpoint — the actual library the capstone rubric names — so you see both the hand-rolled concept and the production tool agree.
Route the batch to production_warehouse/ or quarantine_zone/ based on the DAMA verdict.
Emit both a hand-rolled OpenLineage-style JSON trail and real openlineage-python START/COMPLETE/FAIL events, written to a local file transport (no Marquez server required).


What to look for in the output

The Pydantic contract alone rejects 144,025 of 541,909 rows (26.6%) — the large majority for a missing CustomerID, the rest for non-positive quantities (cancellations) or zero prices.
The DAMA engine, run on the already contract-clean 397,884 rows, still fails — on uniqueness (5,192 exact duplicate rows) and validity (1,838 StockCodes that don’t match the expected 5-digit format). This is the point: a data contract catches record-level violations, but it does not catch duplicates or catalog-format drift — that’s exactly what a broader quality engine (or Great Expectations) is for.
The real Great Expectations checkpoint reports success=True on the same contract-validated rows — because its four expectations (not_be_null, two be_between range checks, and the invoice regex) restate the same rules the Pydantic contract already enforced. It’s a useful confirmation that the two layers agree, not an independent catch.
Because the DAMA verdict is FAILED, the lineage emitters both record a START → FAIL sequence, and the batch is routed to quarantine_zone/ rather than production_warehouse/ — the quality gate actually holding the line, not just logging a warning.







Note



Running this notebook end-to-end in Colab requires a free Kaggle account and API key (Step 2 — Kaggle Authentication), supplied either as Colab Secrets or an uploaded kaggle.json. The dataset itself (carrie1/ecommerce-data, matching the UCI Online Retail Dataset) is public, so some environments can fetch it without credentials — but Colab’s kagglehub calls are written to expect the credentials from Step 2 regardless, so don’t skip that setup.

title: Data Quality: Principles, Validation, and Contracts
text: Computer science has one law that no amount of model size fixes: garbage in, garbage out. You can deploy the most advanced, billion-parameter LLM in the world, but if you feed it corrupted, incomplete, or outdated data, it will confidently produce nonsense — just very fluent nonsense. This is why production-grade data teams don’t treat data quality as a one-time cleaning pass; they build validation frameworks that check every batch, every time, before it reaches a model or a dashboard.

Data Quality: Principles, Validation, and Contracts

title: Data Quality: Principles, Validation, and Contracts
section: The six DAMA dimensions of data quality
text:
The six DAMA dimensions of data quality
When data engineers ask “is this dataset healthy enough to use?”, they don’t guess — they measure it against six standard dimensions, formalized by the DAMA (Data Management Association) data quality framework.








Dimension
What it means
The real-world risk




Accuracy
Data correctly represents real-world ground truth, free of typos or sensor error.
A transposed digit shifts an invoice from $10,000 to $100,000.


Completeness
No critical gaps, missing structural values, or unexpected NULLs.
An AI computes average customer lifetime value while half the history rows are blank.


Consistency
The same entity has the same value everywhere it appears.
One system stores "USA", another stores "United States" — the model treats them as two different countries.


Timeliness / Freshness
Data is current and reflects the real state of operations.
A fraud-detection model trains on three-year-old buying patterns and misses modern attack vectors.


Validity
Values conform to defined business rules, schemas, and ranges.
A column tracking human age contains -5 or 999.


Uniqueness
Every record exists exactly once, no redundant duplicates.
Duplicate customer rows skew training statistics, forcing a model to over-index on repeated behavior.



In short: quality principles describe what “good” looks like; validation techniques (next section) are how you actually check for it.

From principle to query
Each dimension above has a direct, checkable implementation:

Completeness — percentage of non-null values in a critical field. A missing customer_id breaks revenue attribution entirely.
Accuracy — cross-referencing against an authoritative source (does the value match the CRM or ERP record?).
Consistency — the same entity must carry the same value across every system it appears in (an address in the CRM must match the one in the warehouse).
Timeliness — data must land within an agreed SLA window; late financial data can miss a settlement cutoff entirely.
Uniqueness — detected with a simple ratio check: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(DISTINCT id). Any gap between the two is duplicates.
Validity — domain checks such as quantity > 0 or country_code IN ISO 3166-1 alpha-2.

This is exactly the shape of engine you’ll build in today’s lab: six methods, one per dimension, each returning a pass/fail verdict plus a human-readable reason.
crumbs: Day 4 — Data Quality, Governance, and Lineage
Data Quality: Principles, Validation, and Contracts

title: Data Quality: Principles, Validation, and Contracts
text:
Validation techniques
These are the concrete, reusable mechanisms that implement the dimensions above at the code level:

Schema validation — does the record have the right fields, in the right types?
Type validation — is quantity actually numeric, not a string that happens to look numeric?
Range validation — does price fall within a sane business range?
Null / missing value checks — are required fields actually populated?
Duplicate detection — does a natural or primary key repeat?
Pattern validation — does a field match an expected format, such as an email regex or an invoice-number pattern?
Consistency validation — does the same entity agree with itself across tables or systems?

Individually these are simple checks. The engineering discipline is applying all of them, consistently, at the boundary of the pipeline — which is exactly what a data contract formalizes.

title: Data Quality: Principles, Validation, and Contracts
section: Data contracts — formalizing the producer–consumer agreement
text:
Data contracts — formalizing the producer–consumer agreement
A data contract is a machine-enforceable schema plus an SLA between the system that produces data and the system that consumes it. Instead of a producer team silently renaming a column and breaking every downstream job, the contract makes the agreement explicit and enforced in code.
Two common ways to implement one:

Pydantic v2, for validating records at the application/pipeline boundary:
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator, ConfigDict

class OrderContract(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)   # '123' stays a string, never silently becomes 123

    order_id: str
    quantity: float
    email: str

    @field_validator("email")
    @classmethod
    def valid_email(cls, v: str) -> str:
        if "@" not in v:
            raise ValueError("malformed email")
        return v
strict=True blocks silent type coercion — a string '123' is never quietly promoted to the integer 123. Custom @field_validator methods raise on anything else the schema alone can’t express, like a malformed email.
dbt contracts, for enforcing shape at the warehouse/model level: setting enforced: true in a model’s YAML makes the build itself fail the moment a column’s type or name drifts from what’s declared — the disagreement is caught at build time, not by a confused analyst three weeks later.


The violation pipeline
A contract is only useful if violations have a defined path:
validate at ingest → quarantine invalid records → alert the producer → block downstream propagation
Nothing invalid is silently dropped, and nothing invalid is silently allowed through either — it’s set aside, visibly, with the producer notified. Breaking changes to a contract — removing a column, narrowing a type — are treated as major-version changes, with a migration window for consumers before the old shape is retired.
The lab notebook builds exactly this: a RetailTransactionContract Pydantic model that rejects any record with a missing customer ID, a non-positive quantity, or a malformed invoice number, before the DAMA quality engine ever sees it.

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
text:
Ask a large language model something like “What were the key discussion points in our company’s board meeting yesterday?” and it will do one of three things: hallucinate a confident but false answer, admit it doesn’t know (because its training data has a cutoff date), or give a generic non-answer (“board meetings typically discuss strategy and finances…”). None of those are useful, and all three come from the same root causes: the model’s knowledge is static (frozen at training time), it has no memory of your private data (it never saw your internal documents), and it is prone to hallucination (when unsure, it guesses plausibly instead of admitting ignorance).
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) retrieves relevant documents from an external knowledge source — usually a vector database — and injects them into the LLM’s prompt, so the model generates an answer grounded in real, retrieved data rather than in memory alone. It’s the difference between an open-book and a closed-book exam: without RAG, the model answers purely from memory and may hallucinate; with RAG, it looks the answer up first, then answers from what it found. Embeddings and similarity search — covered in Vector Databases and Embeddings — are the fuel and the engine; RAG is the complete vehicle built around them.
Every RAG pipeline runs in three phases: retrieve relevant documents using similarity search, augment the prompt with those documents, and generate an answer grounded in that context.

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
text:
The complete RAG architecture
The full pipeline splits into two steps that run at very different times: indexing, done once offline, and querying, done every time a user asks something.





graph TD
    A["Documents<br>(PDFs, wikis, emails, code)"] --> B["Chunking<br>(split into passages)"]
    B --> C["Embedding<br>(chunk → vector)"]
    C --> D[("Vector DB<br>(chunk + vector + metadata)")]







Phase one: indexing (preparation)
This is the offline step — building the “textbook” the system will later search:








Step
Action
Example




1. Load
Collect all source documents
Company policies, product manuals, support tickets


2. Chunk
Split into semantic units
Each chunk = 512 tokens with 50-token overlap


3. Embed
Generate a vector for each chunk
chunk_vector = embedding_model(chunk_text)


4. Store
Save chunk + vector + metadata
{id: 123, text: "...", vector: [0.1, 0.9, ...], source: "HR_policy.pdf"}





Phase two: querying (inference)
This runs on every user question. For the query “What is our vacation policy?”: embed the query, run similarity search against the vector database to get the top-k nearest chunks (e.g., k=5), retrieve the actual text of those chunks, build a prompt containing system instructions plus the retrieved chunks plus the user’s question, send it to the LLM, and return the generated answer — e.g., “Our vacation policy provides 15 days per year…”

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
text:
Three RAG architecture patterns










Pattern
Flow
Pros
Cons
Use case




1. Naive RAG
Query → Retrieve → Augment → Generate → Answer
Easy to build, works for simple Q&A
No quality checks; retrieves wrong chunks often
Prototypes, internal demos


2. Advanced RAG
Query → rewrite → Retrieve → Rerank → Filter → Augment → Generate
Much higher accuracy
More latency, more components to maintain
Production systems


3. Modular / Agentic RAG
System decides which retriever to call (vector DB, web search, SQL, API); can retrieve iteratively
Most powerful — answers complex multi-hop questions
Complex to build and debug
Multi-hop, tool-using assistants



Advanced RAG adds two things around the naive loop: pre-retrieval processing (rewriting an ambiguous query, expanding it with synonyms) and post-retrieval processing (reranking chunks with a more expensive cross-encoder, filtering out low-quality ones). Modular/agentic RAG goes further still — the system can ask a follow-up question, retrieve again, and chain retrievals together, which is the only way to answer something like “What is the capital of the country where Einstein was born?” (a single retrieval can’t connect those two facts).

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
text:
Walking through a real query
User asks: “How many vacation days do new hires get?”

Embed the query → [0.23, -0.56, 0.78, ...]
Similarity search returns the top 3 chunks: Chunk A (score 0.92, “New hires in their first year receive 10 vacation days”), Chunk B (score 0.88, “Employees with 1–5 years of service receive 15 days”), Chunk C (score 0.45, “Vacation policy was revised in January 2024”).
Reranking (optional): a cross-encoder re-evaluates all three and promotes Chunk A to rank 1, dropping Chunk C entirely as irrelevant noise.
Build the prompt: Context: New hires in their first year receive 10 vacation days. Question: How many vacation days do new hires get? Answer:
LLM generation: “New hires receive 10 vacation days during their first year of employment.”
Return to user.

Notice what happened: the LLM did not “know” this fact. It read it from the retrieved chunk and paraphrased it — that’s the entire point of RAG.

Where basic RAG breaks








Problem
Explanation
Mitigation




Low recall
Relevant chunks not retrieved
Improve chunking, embedding model, or increase k


Low precision
Irrelevant chunks retrieved
Add reranking, metadata filtering


Context window overflow
Retrieved too much text
Compress chunks, use a smaller k


Outdated data
Vector DB hasn’t been updated
Implement incremental indexing


Multi-hop questions
Single retrieval can’t connect separate facts
Use iterative or agentic RAG
