title: Advanced RAG Engineering
text:
Chunking strategies
Imagine splitting a 10-page medical paper into rigid 100-character chunks. One chunk ends with “The patient showed no signs of” and the next begins with “improvement after treatment.” A user asks “Did the patient improve?” and the system retrieves one chunk with no answer, or the other with missing context — either way, a wrong answer. Chunking is the art of breaking documents into pieces that are meaningful, self-contained, and searchable.
Good chunking has three goals: semantic completeness (each chunk should make sense on its own — cutting a sentence in half fails this), appropriate size (small enough for efficient retrieval, large enough to hold context — 50-character chunks lose meaning, 5000-character chunks waste the context window), and contextual boundaries (respect the document’s natural structure — never split inside a table, code block, or list). The golden rule: a chunk should be a unit of meaning — a paragraph, a function — not an arbitrary slice of bytes.









Strategy
How it works
Best for
Avoid for




Fixed-size
Splits every N characters/tokens, regardless of content
Logs, uniform text, unknown structure
Any structured document — it breaks sentences and ideas


Sentence-based
Splits on punctuation boundaries
Conversational text, support tickets
Very long or complex sentences; abbreviations like “Dr. Smith” can fool it


Recursive / hierarchical
Recursively splits by decreasing boundary — document → section → paragraph → sentence — stopping once a chunk is within the target size
Books, manuals, legal documents with clear headings
Flat, unstructured text with no real hierarchy


Semantic
Embeds sliding windows of sentences; splits where similarity between adjacent windows drops sharply
Large, mixed-content documents — textbooks, research papers
Small or simple documents — computationally overkill



Fixed-size, concretely: splitting "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. The dog barks." at a rigid 15 characters produces "The quick brown", " fox jumps ove", "r the lazy dog.", " The dog barks." — note the second and third chunks each cut a word in half. It’s trivial to implement and gives predictable, uniform chunk sizes (a typical parameter choice is 512 tokens with 50 tokens of overlap), which is exactly why it works fine for homogeneous text like news articles or log files — but overlap only patches the symptom, it doesn’t fix the underlying loss of semantic boundaries.
Sentence-based, concretely: "The quick brown fox jumps. The lazy dog sleeps. The cat watches." splits cleanly into three chunks, one per sentence. This is easy to implement with NLP libraries like NLTK or spaCy and preserves grammatical units, but individual sentences can be too short to carry context on their own, and naive splitting has no protection against breaking on a period inside an abbreviation like “Dr. Smith.”
Recursive / hierarchical, concretely: the splitter first checks whether the whole document fits the target size; if not, it descends one level and retries on each piece, e.g.:
Document
  ├── Section 1 (too large)
  │     ├── Paragraph 1 (good size) → keep
  │     └── Paragraph 2 (still too large)
  │           ├── Sentence 1 → keep
  │           └── Sentence 2 → keep
  └── Section 2 (good size) → keep
Recursive chunking keeps a paragraph attached to its section, and a sentence to its paragraph, so the system can store parent-child relationships — but it requires actually parsing the document’s headings. A related, simpler variant — recursive character chunking — looks for structural markers in order (paragraph breaks \n\n, then sentence-ending punctuation, then whitespace) and splits at the highest-priority marker that keeps chunks near the target size; it respects natural text boundaries well for markdown files, blog posts, and essays, but can still separate a chart or table from the paragraph that explains it.
Semantic is the most content-aware of the four: it detects where meaning shifts by comparing the embeddings of consecutive sentence windows, splitting only where similarity drops. Concretely, over five sentences S1..S5, embed each 3-sentence sliding window — Window A = (S1,S2,S3) → vector V1, Window B = (S2,S3,S4) → vector V2, Window C = (S3,S4,S5) → vector V3 — and if similarity(V1, V2) stays high but similarity(V2, V3) drops sharply, that’s a topic shift, so the chunker splits between S3 and S4. This finds natural topic boundaries that structural splitting can’t see, at the cost of running an embedding model during indexing, not just at query time.

Chunk overlap
Regardless of strategy, chunks should almost always overlap — chunk 2 repeats the last few tokens of chunk 1:
Chunk 1: [A B C D E F G]
Chunk 2: [F G H I J K L]   ← overlaps by 2 tokens (F, G)
Chunk 3: [K L M N O P Q]   ← overlaps by 2 tokens (K, L)
Without overlap, “The patient showed no” ends one chunk and “signs of improvement” starts the next, and the LLM never sees the complete sentence. With overlap, both chunks contain the boundary. Recommended overlap is 10–20% of chunk size: 512-token chunks get 50–100 tokens of overlap; 256-token chunks get 25–50.

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
section: Hybrid search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion
text:
Hybrid search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion
Pure vector search misses exact keyword matches — a query for “GPT-4” can retrieve documents about “a language model” instead of the literal string. Pure BM25 (keyword search) misses semantic meaning entirely — “canine therapy” doesn’t match “dog treatment” at all if no words overlap.
Hybrid search runs both a vector ANN search and a BM25 keyword search in parallel, then merges the two result lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF):
\[\text{RRF score} = \sum_{\text{list}} \frac{1}{k + \text{rank}_i}, \quad k = 60\]
RRF rewards a document that ranks highly in both lists, without needing any weights tuned by hand — and empirically it outperforms a weighted linear combination of the two scores in most benchmarks. Most modern vector databases (Weaviate, Elasticsearch, Qdrant) expose hybrid search natively.
crumbs: Day 3 — Vector Databases and Advanced RAG Engineering

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
section: Cross-encoder reranking — the second precision gate
text:
Cross-encoder reranking — the second precision gate
A bi-encoder (the retrieval stage) embeds the query and each document independently — fast, but it can miss subtle relevance because query and document never actually interact during scoring. A cross-encoder (reranking stage) takes the (query, document) pair jointly and scores them together — far more accurate, because it can model the interaction between query tokens and document tokens directly, at the cost of one inference call per candidate (O(n), versus O(1) for bi-encoder similarity).
The standard workflow: retrieve the top 50 candidates cheaply with the bi-encoder, rerank those 50 with the cross-encoder, then pass only the top 3 to 5 to the LLM. Rerank only when retrieval returns more than ~10 candidates — it adds roughly 50–200ms of latency per query. Common models: ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 (fast), bge-reranker-large (more accurate), or a hosted option like the Cohere Rerank API.
crumbs: Day 3 — Vector Databases and Advanced RAG Engineering

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
section: RAG evaluation — the triad you must measure
text:
RAG evaluation — the triad you must measure
You cannot guess whether an architecture change improved retrieval — you have to measure it:

Context Precision — are the retrieved chunks actually relevant? (no noise)
Context Recall — did retrieval find all the chunks needed to answer? (completeness)
Answer Faithfulness — does the generated answer stick to the retrieved context, or does it add facts that weren’t there? (hallucination risk)
Answer Relevance — does the answer actually address what the user asked?

RAGAS is the standard open-source framework: it computes all four metrics automatically using an LLM as judge. A useful alert rule: if faithfulness drops below 0.85, the retrieval or the prompt has regressed and needs attention.
crumbs: Day 3 — Vector Databases and Advanced RAG Engineering

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
text:
Building production-ready RAG pipelines
Turning a working prototype into something stable and accurate at scale means implementing five layers:
[Ingestion Layer] → [Hybrid Retrieval] → [Two-Stage Reranking] → [Data Sync / CDC] → [Evaluation Triad]

The ingestion layer. Production data is rarely clean markdown — it’s multi-column PDFs, scanned documents, and messy financial tables. Modern pipelines use vision-based layout parsers (Docling, Unstructured) to convert these into clean semantic trees that preserve table structure. Every chunk should also be stamped with metadata — file_id, security_clearance_level, creation_date, document_version — you can’t just inject raw text.
Hybrid retrieval. Relying only on vector search is a classic prototype mistake — it struggles with exact product serial numbers, code symbols, or jargon. Combine dense (vector) retrieval with sparse (BM25) retrieval via RRF, as covered above.
Two-stage reranking, to mitigate “lost-in-the-middle”: dumping the top 30 raw chunks into an LLM overwhelms it and it starts ignoring information buried in the middle of the prompt. Stage one fetches the top 50 candidates cheaply; stage two reranks with a cross-encoder and keeps only the best 3–5.
Keeping data fresh — incremental sync and CDC. A production knowledge base isn’t static; a nightly full wipe-and-reindex doesn’t scale.








Sync strategy
How it works
When to use it




Incremental updates
Monitors folder timestamps or commit histories, re-indexes only new/modified documents
Standard corporate files and wikis


Change Data Capture (CDC)
Hooks directly into a live database to mirror inserts/updates/deletes into the vector store instantly
Highly dynamic data — live inventory, ticketing



Continuous evaluation. Score every architectural change against the RAG triad (context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance) — you cannot tell whether a change helped without measuring it.

title: Advanced RAG Engineering
section: Lab: building an advanced RAG system
text:
Lab: building an advanced RAG system
The Day 3 lab notebook implements this entire pipeline end to end over a small built-in knowledge base of data-engineering documents (Kafka, Delta Lake, RAG, HNSW, hybrid search): document chunking, a ChromaDB vector index (HNSW backend), BM25 keyword search, RRF hybrid fusion, cross-encoder reranking, RAG prompt construction, and RAGAS-style precision and similarity evaluation — all on a real, executed run using local, free components (no hosted vector DB, no paid embeddings API, no GPU).
It also demonstrates the two things that make ChromaDB a database rather than just an in-memory index: writing to a PersistentClient, dropping the handle, reopening from disk with zero re-embedding, and narrowing a query with where={"doc_id": ...} metadata filtering before similarity ranking ever runs — the same mechanism a real multi-tenant or access-controlled RAG system uses to keep one customer’s documents out of another’s results.
What to look for in the output:

Candidate counts moving through each stage — vector search, BM25 search, RRF fusion — for four different queries against the same eight-document knowledge base.
The persistence demo: a chunk count that survives reopening the database from disk, and a metadata-filtered query returning fewer candidates, all from one doc_id.
The cross-encoder reranking step narrowing the fused candidates down to the top 3, with each surviving chunk’s text printed.
The final RAG prompt assembled from the top reranked chunks, plus the retrieval metrics (context_precision, avg_similarity) and a pass/fail quality read-out, printed for every query.







Note



The practice exercise covers the same six stages as the lab, but its task cells contain deliberate ??? placeholders for students to fill in — it will not run as delivered, and that is intentional, not a bug. It’s kept as a separate notebook from the worked lab rather than merged into it, since merging would either break the lab’s run-as-delivered state or defeat the exercise’s purpose. title: Day 3 — Vector Databases and Advanced RAG Engineering
text:
For two days we’ve focused on getting data to rest somewhere reliable — a lakehouse table, a stream of validated events. Today we ask a different question: once an AI system needs to reason over that data, how does it find the handful of facts relevant to one specific question, out of millions of documents, in milliseconds?
If you’ve used ChatGPT, Gemini, or any modern AI assistant and wondered how it instantly locates the exact sentence or concept you’re asking about, the answer is a combination of two ideas: embeddings, which turn meaning into geometry, and vector databases, which search that geometry at scale. Together they solve the two things a raw large language model is genuinely bad at — it forgets (a fixed context window) and it hallucinates (it guesses plausibly when it doesn’t actually know). Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the architecture that wires a vector database into an LLM so the model answers from retrieved, grounded facts instead of from memory alone.
Vector databases and advanced RAG sit at the absolute core of production-grade AI systems. A basic RAG system just chops text into blocks and matches keywords — that’s enough for a demo, but it breaks down in production: wrong chunks get retrieved, exact terms get missed, and the model drowns in irrelevant context. Advanced architecture, by contrast, handles millions of high-dimensional vectors with the speed, accuracy, and reasoning capability production systems actually need — hybrid search, reranking, smarter chunking and indexing, and continuous evaluation are the techniques that close that gap.

title: Streaming and Event-Driven Architectures
text:
Picture a busy online bookstore running on yesterday’s architecture: batch processing. Every click, search, and cart addition during the day gets written to a holding area and left untouched. Nothing happens to it until midnight, when an automated job bundles millions of the day’s individual actions into one enormous file, ships it off to be processed, and — by 2 a.m. — the dashboards and inventory counts finally catch up to reality.
That works fine for a monthly financial audit. It fails badly the moment the business needs to react during the day. If a book goes viral on social media at 8 a.m. and sells out by 9, the inventory system won’t know it’s gone until the midnight batch runs — the store spends the rest of the day selling a book it doesn’t have. Batch processing has two structural flaws: insights are always stale (by definition, historical), and cramming 24 hours of computation into one nightly window strains the infrastructure right when it runs.
Streaming replaces the midnight truck with a moving escalator. The instant a customer buys a book, that action becomes an individual, self-contained event — placed directly onto the escalator instead of a holding pen. Processing engines on the other side read, clean, and analyze each event within milliseconds of it happening. Data is never allowed to sit idle.









Batch processing
Streaming




Data unit
A large, bounded file with a clear start and end
An individual, unbounded event


Latency
Hours (the next scheduled run)
Milliseconds


Compute pattern
One heavy burst, usually overnight
Continuous, spread evenly over time


Best for
Historical reports, monthly audits, model retraining
Fraud detection, live personalization, operational alerting


Failure mode
A viral spike goes unnoticed for hours
A single malformed event can be isolated without stopping the flow

title: Streaming and Event-Driven Architectures
section: The architecture: producers, broker, stream processor
text:
The architecture: producers, broker, stream processor
Moving beyond batches means building an event-driven pipeline out of three layers that never talk to each other directly:





graph LR
    P["Producers<br>apps, sensors, GPS trackers"] --> B["Streaming Broker<br>Kafka / Redpanda"]
    B --> S["Stream Processor<br>Flink / Spark Structured Streaming"]
    S --> D["Downstream sinks<br>Delta Lake, dashboards, AI models"]







Producers are whatever generates the live data — a mobile app tap, a factory sensor, a GPS ping. The instant something happens, the producer broadcasts it; it doesn’t wait for anyone to be listening.
The streaming broker is the central station built to absorb millions of simultaneous events without falling over. Tools like Apache Kafka or Redpanda act as an immutable, ordered logbook: events are caught in the exact order they arrived and held safely in line until a consumer reads them.
The stream processor — Apache Flink, or Spark Structured Streaming — sits actively over the moving feed and computes on the fly. It never asks “what was yesterday’s revenue?”; it continuously maintains the answer to “what is revenue as of this exact second?”


Why this matters

Ride-hailing (Uber/Careem). If ETA and fare calculation ran as a nightly batch, the app would be useless. Instead, your phone streams location continuously; the broker catches it, and a stream processor recomputes your ETA and fare every second.
Financial fraud detection. A batch system discovers a stolen card hours after the fact. A streaming system consumes the swipe event, scores it for anomalies, and can freeze the account before the transaction even clears.
Instant personalization. Streaming pipelines feed live clicks directly into recommendation models — click on three football clips and your next scroll already reflects it, instead of waiting for tomorrow’s batch job.

In short, moving beyond batches shifts infrastructure from a reactive state (analyzing history) to an active one (reacting to the present).

title: Streaming and Event-Driven Architectures
text:
Event-driven architectures for AI systems
Traditional software mostly talks in synchronous request-response — standard REST APIs. Component A calls an AI service and sits completely idle, blocking a thread, until the model finishes computing an answer. That model worked fine when “the AI service” was a fast lookup. It breaks down once AI workloads mean heavy LLM inference, multi-agent orchestration, and continuous streaming data — request-response buckles under the combined weight of high latency and tight coupling between services.
An Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) flips the paradigm: instead of issuing direct commands, components publish and consume events — structured records stating that something happened — through a central broker. Nothing blocks. Producers fire an event and move on; consumers, including AI models, process it whenever they’re ready, and can scale independently based on how deep the backlog gets.








Design dimension
Traditional request-response (REST)
Event-driven architecture (EDA)




Handling LLM latency
Poor — a connection stays open for seconds/minutes during inference, risking timeouts and wasted compute
Excellent — the task is accepted instantly; inference happens asynchronously in the background


System coupling
Tight — if the LLM provider goes down, the calling app crashes immediately
Loose — the broker holds messages safely until the AI service is back


Resource scaling
Rigid — hard to scale compute dynamically for bursty query traffic
Elastic — if the inference-topic queue grows, Kubernetes can spin up 50 extra GPU worker containers on demand to clear the backlog


Extensibility
Hard — a new feature means editing the core application
Easy — hook a new consumer onto the existing broker topic, no other code touched




Core architectural components
An event-driven AI system relies on four structural layers:

Event producers — applications, users, or databases that capture an action (a chat message, a file upload) and broadcast it as a structured event.
The event broker — the high-throughput backbone (Kafka, Redpanda) that receives, orders, and durably stores events without losing any.
AI event consumers — independent workers that listen on specific topics, run AI processing (embeddings, LLM inference) on each event, and emit new event payloads downstream.
Downstream storage sinks and output gateways — where processed AI output lands: a Delta Lake table, a vector database, or a live push back to a user interface.

A minimal version of this pattern — a broker built from nothing more than asyncio.Queue per topic, a producer that never blocks on the consumer, and an AI-processing consumer reading off it — looks like this:
class MockEventBroker:
    def __init__(self):
        self.topics = {
            "raw_support_queries": asyncio.Queue(),
            "processed_embeddings": asyncio.Queue(),
            "ai_agent_responses": asyncio.Queue(),
        }

    async def publish(self, topic, message):
        await self.topics[topic].put(message)

    async def consume(self, topic):
        return await self.topics[topic].get()
This backs a small three-stage, multi-agent pipeline built entirely on asyncio: a Producer emits raw support queries onto the first topic, an Embedding Agent consumes them, chunks and embeds the text, and republishes the result onto processed_embeddings, and an Inference Agent consumes that and runs its own autonomous response strategy, publishing the final answer onto ai_agent_responses. Each hop between agents is just another publish/consume pair on its own queue — which is why the broker needs three topic channels, not two.
The producer calls publish() and immediately goes back to work — it never waits to see what the embedding or inference consumer does with the message. That decoupling is the entire point: swap the asyncio.Queue for a real Kafka topic and the architecture doesn’t change, only the durability and throughput guarantees do. The lab’s MockKafkaBroker (in Day2_Lab.ipynb) builds on exactly this idea, adding partitions and offsets to mirror real Kafka’s semantics.
In short: an event-driven architecture lets independent AI components — producers, embedding workers, inference agents — communicate by publishing and reacting to events instead of waiting idly on each other, which is what lets a production system absorb slow, unpredictable LLM latency without tipping over.

title: Warehouses, Lakes, and Lakehouses
text:
To understand where we are today, we have to look at how data storage evolved. Historically, organizations moved through three distinct eras.





graph LR
    A["Enterprise Data Warehouse<br>1990s–2010s"] --> B["Data Lake<br>2010s–2020s"]
    B --> C["Data Lakehouse<br>Present"]






The Enterprise Data Warehouse (EDW) era (1990s–2010s). Companies stored clean, highly structured data in rigid SQL databases. It was excellent for generating basic business reports, but it was incredibly expensive to scale and completely incapable of handling unstructured data like audio, video, or massive JSON logs.
The Data Lake era (2010s–2020s). With the birth of Hadoop and cloud object storage (like Amazon S3), companies started dumping everything — raw, structured, and unstructured data — into a cheap storage pool. While scalable, these lakes lacked control. With no data validation or transactional safety, they quickly degraded into disorganized “data swamps.”
The Modern Data Lakehouse era (present). This is the current gold standard. A Lakehouse implements a specialized storage layer — open-source columnar frameworks like Delta Lake or Apache Iceberg — directly on top of cheap cloud storage. It gives you the best of both worlds: the ultra-low cost and flexibility of a Data Lake, combined with the strict reliability, schema enforcement, and ACID transactions of a traditional Data Warehouse.

title: Warehouses, Lakes, and Lakehouses
section: Core architectural principle: decoupling compute from storage
text:
Core architectural principle: decoupling compute from storage
In legacy systems, Compute (the processor that does the heavy lifting, calculating, and transforming) and Storage (the hard drives where the raw data sits) were physically bundled inside the same server box. If you ran out of processing power, you had to buy more storage. If you ran out of storage, you had to buy more processors. It was expensive and wasteful.
A modern data architecture completely unties these two components so they can live in separate places and scale independently:

The storage layer. All your data — petabytes of text, numbers, images, video — is dumped into an ultra-cheap, infinitely expandable cloud storage “lake” (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage). It just sits there safely, requiring almost zero electricity or processing power just to hold the data, so it costs pennies.
The compute layer. Processing engines (Apache Spark, Databricks) live entirely separately. When a data scientist or an AI model needs to run a massive computation, a cluster of virtual computers instantly wakes up, hooks into the storage layer, pulls the exact data it needs, processes it in parallel, and delivers the answer.


Why this matters

Massive cost savings. If your company collects data 24/7 but only runs heavy AI models or reports once a week, you don’t need thousands of expensive processors sitting idle all week. You pay a tiny fee to store the data, spin up 100 virtual computers for the 2 hours it takes to run your AI models, and then shut them down completely — you pay for compute by the second it actually runs.
Infinite scalability. If a sudden business need requires analyzing 10 years of data by tomorrow morning, you don’t buy new hardware — you command 500 cloud computers to team up, attack the storage lake simultaneously, finish in minutes, and disappear.
No single point of failure. Because your data isn’t trapped inside the specific computer doing the work, a crashed compute server doesn’t lose or corrupt anything. The data is safe in the storage layer, and another compute server can instantly step in.

In short: decoupling compute from storage turns your data infrastructure from a rigid, expensive box into a flexible system where storage is your permanent memory bank, and compute is a powerful muscle you only flex — and pay for — exactly when you need it.

title: Warehouses, Lakes, and Lakehouses
section: Data ingestion: the revolution of ELT over ETL
text:
Data ingestion: the revolution of ELT over ETL
Both ETL and ELT move raw data from its sources (a mobile app, a website, a database) into a central storage system where data scientists and AI models can use it. The letters stand for:

Extract — gathering the raw data from its source
Load — sending the data to its destination
Transform — cleaning, formatting, and preparing the data

The revolution comes down to flipping the order of the last two steps.
The traditional way — ETL (Extract → Transform → Load). Extract grabs raw data directly from production databases. Because legacy database storage was expensive, engineers then used a separate middle-tier server to clean, aggregate, and shrink the data before storing it, then pushed the pre-formatted, clean data into a rigid Data Warehouse.
The modern way — ELT (Extract → Load → Transform). Pull raw, messy data from all company sources and instantly dump it into a cloud data pool (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Snowflake) in its native, raw state — JSON, Parquet, CSV, no changes made. When analysts or AI models need the data, distributed compute engines (Apache Spark, dbt) transform and clean it inside the storage destination itself, on demand.








Feature
Legacy ETL
Modern ELT




Speed of ingestion
Slow — data waits to be transformed before it can be saved
Ultra-fast — raw data is dumped into storage within seconds


Data preservation
Lossy — raw details are thrown away during transformation
Preserved — 100% of raw historical data is saved forever


Flexibility
Low — changing the pipeline means redesigning the whole system
High — a new format is just a new query against the raw data


Failure recovery
Hard — a mid-pipeline failure can lose or strand data
Easy — raw data stays safe in storage; fix the script and rerun



In short, the revolution of ELT over ETL is a shift from “clean it before you keep it” to “keep it all, and clean it whenever you need it.” By leveraging cheap cloud storage and massive compute, ELT ensures modern AI systems always have access to a rich, uninterrupted history of raw information.

title: Warehouses, Lakes, and Lakehouses
text:
ACID transactions
ACID — Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — is a fundamental set of four safety properties that guarantee database operations remain reliable and error-free, even during sudden crashes, power failures, or simultaneous user errors. A transaction is a sequence of multiple database actions treated as a single logical unit of work.
Without ACID guardrails, if a multi-step update hits a network glitch halfway through, the system can save a partial, broken file that permanently corrupts your records. ACID compliance protects the whole ecosystem from data corruption by treating data mutations with strict, absolute validation rules:

Atomicity — an all-or-nothing rule. If a pipeline updating 100 rows fails on row 99, the entire operation is rolled back as if it never happened. No partial writes.
Consistency — any data written strictly obeys predefined structural blueprints, schema enforcement, and database constraints before it’s committed to storage.
Isolation — when multiple pipelines or users concurrently modify the same data lake, their transactions run independently without overlapping or cross-contaminating each other’s live files.
Durability — once a transaction is successfully written, its changes are permanently recorded in non-volatile storage and transaction logs. The clean data is never lost, even after a catastrophic power failure.

title: Warehouses, Lakes, and Lakehouses
text:
Delta Lake
Delta Lake is an open-source storage management layer installed directly on top of a standard cloud data lake (Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage) to turn it into a highly organized, reliable Data Lakehouse. Historically, data lakes let companies store massive volumes of raw files cheaply, but they lacked management controls and degraded into “data swamps” where simultaneous file updates could corrupt information. Delta Lake fixes this by wrapping raw files in a protective engine that brings database-style reliability, strict data quality controls, and fast SQL query performance to your existing cloud storage — all while keeping the lake’s ultra-low operational cost.
The engine achieves this through three core technical guardrails:

ACID compliance — an all-or-nothing gatekeeper. If a computer crashes mid-pipeline, a half-written file is safely rolled back instead of permanently corrupting the database.
The Delta Log — a hidden central ledger recording a perfect historical diary of every data mutation. This powers Time Travel, letting engineers instantly query or restore the dataset exactly as it looked at any point in the past.
Schema enforcement — validates the structure of all incoming streams at the door, blocking malformed data before it can crash downstream ML models or dashboards.

You don’t choose between Delta Lake and ACID transactions — you use Delta Lake because it provides ACID transactions on top of cheap cloud object storage. It turns a chaotic, unsafe data lake into a reliable, enterprise-ready lakehouse.









Delta Lake
ACID transactions




What is it?
An open-source storage layer built on top of file systems
A theoretical standard of data integrity and reliability


Implementation
You install it, write code with it, and store files (Delta tables)
A checklist of guarantees implemented by the storage engine


Mechanism
Parquet files + an immutable _delta_log file tracker
Write-ahead logs, locking mechanisms, isolation levels


Scope
Specific to the Big Data / Cloud Lakehouse ecosystem
Applies globally to all databases, financial systems, storage engines




The Delta transaction log: how ACID actually works
_delta_log/ is a hidden directory of JSON commit files at the root of every Delta table. Each commit is one atomic operation — add new Parquet files, remove old ones, never a partial write. The read protocol replays every commit from version 0 to reconstruct the current table state.
Writers use optimistic concurrency control: they check for conflicting commits before finalizing a write. If two writers race on the same partition, one wins and one retries — no corruption, no data loss. This is how Delta guarantees ACID without a traditional database engine underneath it.
After every 10 commits, Delta writes a checkpoint.parquet so readers don’t have to replay thousands of JSON files on startup — this is Delta Log compaction.


MERGE / UPSERT — why overwrite is not enough
A raw overwrite rewrites the entire table for one changed row: O(n) cost, no history, unsafe under concurrency. MERGE is the operation that makes atomic upserts possible:
MERGE INTO target USING source ON condition
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT
Delta executes MERGE atomically: it scans only the affected files, writes new Parquet, and logs the operation. The typical use case is CDC (Change Data Capture) — applying inserts, updates, and deletes from a source system in one pass. Predicate pushdown lets Delta skip files whose min/max stats prove no matching rows exist, which is a massive speedup. Combine MERGE with timestamp columns for SCD Type 2 — full history without duplicates or missing records.


OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER BY — data skipping
Streaming writes create thousands of tiny Parquet files — the small files problem — and each file read is a separate I/O operation that kills query scan time.

OPTIMIZE table compacts small files into larger ones (default target ~1 GB) within each partition.
Z-ORDER BY (col1, col2) co-locates related values in the same files using space-filling curves. Every file’s _delta_log entry records min/max stats per column, so a reader skips irrelevant files entirely — e.g. WHERE country = 'SA' reads under 5% of files if the table is Z-ordered by country.

Schedule OPTIMIZE weekly or after bulk loads — running it too frequently has diminishing returns.


VACUUM and Time Travel — storage management
Old Parquet files stay on disk until explicitly cleaned; Delta just stops referencing them. That’s what makes Time Travel possible:
SELECT * FROM table VERSION AS OF 5
SELECT * FROM table TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-01-01'
VACUUM table RETAIN 168 HOURS deletes files older than the retention window (default 7 days). VACUUM is irreversible — deleted files cannot be restored from Delta. Never vacuum below 7 days if streaming readers are still active; they may reference older offsets. Longer retention means richer time travel history, at the cost of a higher object storage bill.


Schema evolution — handling upstream changes
By default, Delta rejects writes with schema mismatches — this protects downstream queries from silent corruption. To opt in to schema evolution:

spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled", "true")
mergeSchema=True on write — adds new columns from the source, never drops existing ones.
overwriteSchema=True — a full schema replacement, for intentional breaking changes only.

Schema enforcement happens at write time, not read time — errors surface at the producer, not the consumer. Best practice: version schema changes, and notify consumers before adding NOT NULL columns or renaming fields.

title: Day 1 — Foundations of Data Engineering for AI
text:
Before a model can be trained, before a feature vector can be computed, before making any prediction — data must move. It must be collected, cleaned, transformed, validated, and delivered reliably. Data engineering is that discipline.
If you look at the field of Artificial Intelligence and Data Science today, everyone talks about the glamorous side: training Large Language Models, running neural networks, and building autonomous agents. But here is the industry’s open secret: an AI model is only as smart as the data you feed it. Without data engineers building the invisible roads, pipes, and purification systems, data remains trapped, messy, and useless.
This course gives you a complete mental model of modern data engineering for AI systems — how pipelines are designed, where they break, what patterns experienced engineers use to make them reliable, and how the data layer connects to every other part of the ML system.

title: Day 2 — Real-Time Data Pipelines
text:
Yesterday we decoupled storage from compute and settled the ETL-vs-ELT question. Both of those still assumed a comfortable premise: data arrives, sits somewhere, and gets processed later. Today we break that premise.
Most of the data an AI system actually cares about — a user’s click, a sensor reading, a credit-card swipe, a server logging an error, a chat message arriving mid-conversation — is not useful “later.” A fraud model that flags a stolen card six hours after the purchase has already failed. A recommendation engine that updates your feed once a day feels broken compared to one that adapts on your very next scroll. Real-time data engineering is the discipline of treating data as a continuous, never-ending flow of individual events, and processing each one within milliseconds of it happening — not storing it to process in bulk tonight. Concretely, that means extracting each event the instant it’s generated, transmitting it, cleaning and enriching it, and delivering it to its final destination, all within fractions of a second.
This matters even more once AI is in the loop. LLM inference is slow relative to a database query — a call can take seconds, not milliseconds — and multi-agent systems chain many of those calls together. A traditional synchronous request-response design blocks a whole thread on every one of them. Event-driven, streaming architectures are how production AI systems absorb that latency without falling over: producers publish events and move on, brokers hold the backlog safely, and consumers — including AI models — process at their own pace, scaling up or down independently.

title: Building Real-Time Pipelines
text: Building a production-grade streaming pipeline is a complete departure from batch engineering. System changes — a user click, an IoT temperature spike, a financial transaction — are instantly broadcast as individual event objects, typically structured as JSON, Avro, or Protobuf payloads, rather than waiting to land in a daily export. Data is no longer a bounded file with a beginning and an end — it’s an unbounded dataset: a continuous, append-only series of events that never finishes arriving. Producers and consumers stay loosely coupled, talking only through the broker, never directly to each other. To design for that, engineers need to understand what actually happens inside the broker and the processor sitting on top of it.

title: Building Real-Time Pipelines
section: A minimal streaming pipeline in Python
text:
A minimal streaming pipeline in Python
Before reaching for Kafka itself, it’s worth seeing the same producer / broker / processor shape in miniature. This small simulator swaps Kafka for a plain asyncio.Queue per topic channel:
import asyncio
import json
import random
from datetime import datetime

# Simulating a High-Throughput Distributed Message Broker
class StreamBroker:
    def __init__(self):
        # Different message topic channels
        self.topics = {
            "iot_sensor_stream": asyncio.Queue(),
            "processed_alerts": asyncio.Queue(),
        }

    async def publish(self, topic, message):
        await self.topics[topic].put(message)

    async def consume(self, topic):
        return await self.topics[topic].get()
temperature_sensor_producer emits unstructured readings from two independent sensors, SENSOR_A and SENSOR_B, onto iot_sensor_stream, smoothly and without caring who — if anyone — is reading them. StreamBroker itself handles the concurrent ingress of both streams safely; it doesn’t know or care that two producers are publishing at once, since each call just drops a message onto the appropriate queue. On the other side, anomaly_detection_stream_processor consumes from that same queue and parses each incoming event in real time, running an instant mathematical threshold check and publishing anything that trips it onto processed_alerts — all without ever storing data in an intermediate relational table.

title: Building Real-Time Pipelines
section: Kafka: partitions, offsets, and consumer groups
text:
Kafka: partitions, offsets, and consumer groups
A Kafka topic isn’t a single log — it’s split into N ordered, immutable partitions, and every message is routed to exactly one of them. Within a partition, each message gets a monotonically increasing offset, which is simply its address: “message #4,213 in partition 2.”
Consumers read as a consumer group: a set of workers that jointly consume a topic, with every partition assigned to exactly one member of the group at a time. That assignment is what sets the pipeline’s real throughput ceiling — adding consumers beyond the partition count gives zero extra parallelism, because there’s nothing left to hand them.








Concept
What it is
Why it matters




Partition
One ordered, immutable log within a topic
Unit of parallelism — more partitions, more concurrent consumers


Offset
A message’s position within its partition
Lets a consumer say exactly where it is


Consumer group
A set of consumers sharing a topic’s partitions
Each partition goes to one member only


Offset commit
A consumer checkpoints its current position
Crash recovery resumes from the last committed offset, not from zero


Rebalance
Partition reassignment when a member joins or leaves
Keeps the group’s load balanced automatically

title: Building Real-Time Pipelines
text:
Window types: tumbling, sliding, session
A stream never “ends,” so aggregations (sums, averages, counts) need a boundary to close over. That boundary is a window, and the three common shapes solve different problems:








Window type
Shape
Use case




Tumbling
Fixed-size, non-overlapping — every event belongs to exactly one window
Hourly sales totals — clean, non-overlapping reporting periods


Sliding
Fixed-size, overlapping — one event can appear in multiple windows
Rolling 5-minute average CPU load — overlap is needed to catch a spike right at a window boundary


Session
Gap-based — the window closes after N seconds of inactivity; size varies per session
Click-stream grouping — a user’s session ends after 30+ minutes idle



The lab’s StreamProcessor (in Day2_Lab.ipynb) implements both a tumbling window (one-second buckets, used for a per-second event count) and a sliding window (a rolling 3-second average temperature) side by side over the same event stream, so you can see both update independently as events arrive.

title: Building Real-Time Pipelines
text:
Watermarks: handling late-arriving data
Network delays mean an event timestamped T can physically arrive at the processor at T + 5 minutes. A watermark is a declared threshold that answers “how long am I willing to wait for a late event before I close the window and move on?” — in Spark Structured Streaming:
stream.withWatermark("event_time", "5 minutes")
Anything that arrives after the watermark has already passed is either dropped or routed to a dead-letter side output. The trade-off is direct: a larger watermark buys more completeness at the cost of higher latency; a smaller one returns results faster but drops more late data. Set it from the observed p99 latency of the actual data source — not the theoretical worst case, which would make every window wait far longer than necessary.

title: Building Real-Time Pipelines
text:
Exactly-once delivery — the hard problem
Every streaming system has to pick a delivery guarantee, and the honest options trade off against each other:








Guarantee
Behavior
Cost




At-most-once
Fire and forget
Fastest, but silent data loss on failure — never acceptable for financial or audit data


At-least-once
Retry on failure
No data loss, but duplicates are possible — the most common default


Exactly-once
No loss, no duplicates
Requires coordination between producer, broker, and consumer



Kafka reaches exactly-once with enable.idempotence=true, the transactional producer API, and isolation.level=read_committed on the consumer side. Flink reaches it with two-phase-commit checkpointing, which only works if the sink itself supports transactions (Kafka, JDBC, Iceberg all do). Either way, exactly-once isn’t free — it adds roughly 20% throughput overhead — so pay for it only where a duplicate would cause real harm (a double-charged payment, a double-counted fraud alert), not for every topic in the system by default.

title: Building Real-Time Pipelines
text:
Ingestion, transformation, orchestration
Every pipeline — batch or streaming — still breaks down into the same three stages; only the tools and latency budget change.








Stage
Purpose
Typical tools




Ingestion
Pull raw data from external systems into central storage
Apache Kafka, Debezium, Fivetran, AWS Kinesis


Transformation
Clean, filter, and structure the raw data
Apache Spark, dbt, PySpark, Pandas


Orchestration
Schedule tasks, manage dependencies, handle errors across the whole system
Apache Airflow, Prefect, Dagster



Ingestion is the vacuum cleaner gathering raw material — user clicks, database updates, application logs — from wherever it’s generated into central storage. Transformation is the factory turning that raw material into a usable product: filtering out noise, deduplicating records, and converting messy raw files into the standard tables downstream AI models and analytical tools can actually read. Orchestration is the conductor making sure every stage runs in the right order and recovers cleanly when something fails.

section: Lab: a real-time streaming pipeline with Kafka and Delta Lake
text:
Lab: a real-time streaming pipeline with Kafka and Delta Lake
The Day 2 lab notebook puts every concept above into one runnable pipeline, in two parts. It leans on asyncio for the concurrent streaming loops, pins pyspark==3.5.0 alongside delta-spark==3.5.0 to manage the Lakehouse storage sink, and otherwise sticks to the standard library for the math.
Part 1 — mock Kafka streaming pipeline. A MockKafkaBroker (built on asyncio.Queue, with partitions and offsets modeled explicitly) receives readings from three concurrent factory-sensor producers (CNC_MILL_01, ROBOTIC_ARM_02, ASSEMBLY_LINE_03), each flooding the broker independently without talking to each other or locking on any shared thread state. A StreamProcessor consumes them and applies all three concepts from this page at once: a tumbling window (per-second event counts), a sliding window (a 3-second rolling average that keeps readings in memory only for that active span and evicts anything older to keep memory bounded), and a watermark (dropping anything older than 2 seconds). Anything over threshold gets published to an anomalies_sink topic, which a Delta Lake writer appends transactionally, turning the transient micro-batches back into durable, queryable structured logs — the same ACID guarantees from Day 1, now on a live stream instead of a static file.
Part 2 — a real Kafka round trip. The mock broker never touches the actual kafka-python client, and a real capstone pipeline needs schema validation at the edge. This part runs one real KafkaProducer → topic → KafkaConsumer round trip, gated by a Pydantic model (SensorReading) that rejects a deliberately malformed message (a temperature sent as the string "not_a_number") instead of letting it crash the consumer.






Note



Running Part 1’s Delta sink locally on Windows requires a winutils.exe / HADOOP_HOME setup for PySpark — a standard PySpark-on-Windows limitation, not a bug in the notebook (see the same caveat on Day 1). It runs cleanly on Colab (Linux) or macOS/Linux with no extra setup. The notebook’s own saved output for Part 1 was captured from a real executed run on Colab.








Note



Part 2 needs a real, running Kafka broker on localhost:9092 — the notebook includes the commands to start a local single-broker Kafka directly in Colab (KRaft mode, no Zookeeper needed). The output saved in this notebook was captured from a real run against a live broker, and it is the full accept/reject round trip: the producer sends two valid readings and one deliberately malformed one (temperature as the string "not_a_number"), and the consumer accepts the two valid readings, rejects the malformed one on SensorReading’s validator, and ends with Summary: 2 accepted, 1 rejected by the schema gate. If you run this cell without a broker running, you’ll see a connection failure instead — the schema-gate code catches that case and prints clear setup instructions rather than a raw stack trace, but that’s not what the saved output here shows.

title: Vector Databases and Embeddings
text:
An embedding is a numerical representation of data — text, an image, a sound clip — as a list of numbers called a vector. It’s an AI technique that converts a word, a sentence, or a whole document into a long string of numbers, and you can think of those numbers as coordinates on a massive, multidimensional map.
Imagine a map of the world: Cairo and Alexandria sit close together because they’re physically close. An embedding model does the same thing, but for meaning instead of geography. The words “King” and “Queen” land at nearly the same coordinates because they both represent royalty. “I’m feeling down” and “I am sad” sit right next to each other even though the two sentences don’t share a single word. Concretely, “King” might embed as [0.12, -0.45, 0.78, ..., 0.33] (384 numbers long, for a typical small embedding model) and “Queen” as [0.14, -0.43, 0.77, ..., 0.31] — the vectors are close because the meanings are close. Semantic similarity equals distance proximity.
Embeddings capture relationships, not just definitions. The classic word2vec example: in embedding space, "Paris" - "France" + "Italy" lands very close to "Rome". In short: an embedding turns a human concept into a mathematical location.

title: Vector Databases and Embeddings
text:
An embedding is a numerical representation of data — text, an image, a sound clip — as a list of numbers called a vector. It’s an AI technique that converts a word, a sentence, or a whole document into a long string of numbers, and you can think of those numbers as coordinates on a massive, multidimensional map.
Imagine a map of the world: Cairo and Alexandria sit close together because they’re physically close. An embedding model does the same thing, but for meaning instead of geography. The words “King” and “Queen” land at nearly the same coordinates because they both represent royalty. “I’m feeling down” and “I am sad” sit right next to each other even though the two sentences don’t share a single word. Concretely, “King” might embed as [0.12, -0.45, 0.78, ..., 0.33] (384 numbers long, for a typical small embedding model) and “Queen” as [0.14, -0.43, 0.77, ..., 0.31] — the vectors are close because the meanings are close. Semantic similarity equals distance proximity.
Embeddings capture relationships, not just definitions. The classic word2vec example: in embedding space, "Paris" - "France" + "Italy" lands very close to "Rome". In short: an embedding turns a human concept into a mathematical location.

title: Vector Databases and Embeddings
text:
What is a vector database?
A traditional database — a spreadsheet, a SQL table — is built for exact matches: look up a specific order ID, a specific phone number. Ask it to “find documents about a happy puppy” and it has to scan every row of text looking for those literal words, missing anything phrased as “a joyful young dog.” That’s slow, and it’s blind to meaning.
A vector database is built differently. It stores the embeddings themselves — those long coordinate strings — and when you ask it a question, it doesn’t read the text at all. It converts your question into a coordinate, drops that point onto the map, and asks: what are the closest items surrounding this point? This is called similarity search or nearest neighbor search, and because it relies on geometry rather than reading text line by line, a vector database can search billions of documents in milliseconds.





graph LR
    Q["Your question"] --> E["Embedding model"]
    E --> V["Query vector"]
    V --> DB[("Vector database<br>(indexed embeddings)")]
    DB --> R["Nearest-neighbor matches"]






Purpose-built, a vector database exists to do three things: store millions or billions of embedding vectors, index them with algorithms like HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) so search stays fast at scale, and answer a query by embedding it with the same model used on the stored documents, then finding its nearest neighbors.

How the search actually runs, in three steps

Indexing (preparation). Before any query arrives, the database builds a graph or clustering structure over every stored vector, so it never has to brute-force scan the whole collection later. Common index types: HNSW (a layered graph) and IVF (clusters vectors into buckets, like a phonebook divided by city).
Querying (search). Your text query is embedded with the same model used at indexing time, then the system asks which stored vectors are closest to that query vector, using a distance metric.
Retrieval (result). The database returns the top-k most similar items — say, the top 5 chunks — which are then handed to the LLM in a RAG system to generate an answer.



Distance metrics








Metric
What it measures
Best for




Cosine similarity
Angle between vectors (ignores magnitude)
Text embeddings, where document length shouldn’t dominate


Euclidean distance
Straight-line distance
Low-dimensional, numeric data


Dot product
Magnitude × direction
When vector length matters (e.g., recommendation scores)



Cosine similarity is the default for text: it ranges from −1 (opposite meaning) to +1 (identical meaning), and two vectors pointing the same direction score as highly similar even if one document is much longer than the other.


A concrete worked example
Suppose a vector database stores three sentences, each reduced here to a simplified 3-dimensional embedding for illustration:



ID
Text
Embedding (simplified 3D)




1
“The sky is blue”
[0.9, 0.1, 0.2]


2
“Grass is green”
[0.1, 0.9, 0.1]


3
“The ocean is deep”
[0.8, 0.2, 0.3]



A query about the sky would embed close to [0.9, 0.1, 0.2], land nearest to sentence 1, and land second-nearest to sentence 3 — “the ocean is deep” — not because the words overlap, but because both sentences describe a similarly-colored, similarly-toned natural scene. Sentence 2 sits far away in this tiny 3D space, exactly like “grass is green” is a different topic. Real embedding models don’t use 3 dimensions — they typically use hundreds — but the geometry works identically at scale.


Why this matters
Without vector databases and embeddings, LLMs have two structural flaws: they forget (a fixed context window can’t hold a company’s entire knowledge base) and they hallucinate (when unsure, they guess plausibly rather than admit ignorance). A vector database gives an LLM the equivalent of an open-book exam — instead of relying purely on what it memorized during training, it can look up the exact relevant passage first, then answer from that. This pairing is exactly what RAG (covered on the next page) is built on.

title: Vector Databases and Embeddings
text:
Document indexing: two different layers
“Indexing” gets used loosely, but in a vector database context it actually refers to two separate layers: how chunks are logically organized so the LLM gets the cleanest context, and how vectors are physically stored so the search itself is fast. Chunking (splitting documents into pieces) happens before indexing; indexing is what the database does with those chunks once it has them.

Logical / data indexing strategies
These strategies decide how retrieved text connects back to its source, to maximize what the LLM actually sees:

Single-level (flat) indexing. The simplest style — every chunk is an independent vector, and the system fetches the top matches and passes them straight to the LLM.
Parent-child (hierarchical) indexing. Small child chunks (sentences) are indexed for precision search, but each is linked to a larger parent chunk (a paragraph). The system searches the precise child vectors but returns the more context-rich parent text to the LLM.
Hypothetical question indexing. An LLM pre-reads every document and generates several questions a user might plausibly ask about it. Those questions — not the raw text — are what gets embedded and indexed. A real user question then matches against a question that’s phrased the way users actually phrase things.
Summary / document indexing. Instead of indexing raw paragraphs, an LLM writes a high-level summary of each whole document. The system searches summaries first to find the right document, then drills into that document’s specific chunks.
Knowledge graph indexing. Extracts entities as nodes and relationships as edges, so the system can answer questions that require connecting facts scattered across separate documents — something flat chunk retrieval can’t do on its own.



Physical / algorithmic indexing strategies
These are the actual Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms — trading a small amount of mathematical precision for a large gain in search speed:











Strategy
Accuracy
Speed
Memory
Training required?
Use case




Flat (no index)
Exact
Very slow — O(N)
Low
No
Under 10K vectors


IVF

Fast
Moderate
Yes (k-means)

HNSW
Very high
Very fast
High

Approximate

Flat brute-forces the exact distance to every vector — perfect accuracy, but only viable on tiny collections.
IVF (Inverted File Index) clusters the vector space with k-means into “buckets” (Voronoi cells); a query only searches the bucket its own vector falls closest to, at the cost of some accuracy.
HNSW builds a multi-layer graph, like an express subway line — the search takes big leaps across the top layer, then drops down layers to fine-tune the exact match. It’s what Pinecone, Weaviate, and ChromaDB use by default.
PQ (Product Quantization) compresses each vector into small approximate sub-vector codes, shrinking memory by up to 95% — often paired with IVF as IVF-PQ for billion-scale collections.
ScaNN, Google’s index, optimizes anisotropic vector distances to favor vectors that align cleanly with the query’s direction, for hyper-scale production search.

A simple decision path: under 10K vectors, use Flat (no training, exact). Need over 99% accuracy and have the RAM for it, use HNSW. Have over 10M vectors and limited RAM, use IVF+PQ. Operating at Google scale, consider ScaNN.


Tuning HNSW: precision vs. speed
Since HNSW is the default in most production vector databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, ChromaDB), its three parameters are worth knowing by name:

M — bi-directional links per node. Higher M means better recall but more memory (typical range: 16–64).
ef_construction — candidate list size while the index is being built. Higher means a better-quality index, but a slower build.
ef (search) — candidate list size at query time. Higher means better recall but slower search — this is the one you tune per query, at runtime.

The trade-off is concrete: ef=10 is fast but only around 85% recall; ef=200 is slow but around 99% recall. Rule of thumb: tune M and ef_construction once, at build time; tune ef per query’s latency budget, at runtime.

title: Vector Databases and Embeddings
text:
Semantic search and similarity search
Keyword search — the traditional approach — matches exact words or substrings: LIKE clauses, inverted indexes, boolean logic. A query for “car” retrieves only documents containing the literal string “car.” Search for “canine therapy” on a site whose articles only say “dog healing,” and you get zero results, even though the content is exactly what you wanted. Keyword search is blind to meaning: it misses synonyms (“automobile” vs. “car”), misses context (is “Jaguar” an animal, a car, or an OS?), word order matters in brittle ways, and it breaks on polysemy — one word, many meanings.
Semantic search understands the intent behind a query rather than its literal words. “Ways to calm a nervous dog” retrieves documents about “reducing canine anxiety” or “soothing an agitated pet” even though none of those exact words match. It handles synonyms, concept matching (“cold weather” ↔︎ “winter conditions”), and phrasing variation (“How do I…” ↔︎ “What is the method for…”). Semantic search is conceptual: it maps queries and documents into a shared meaning space.
Similarity search is the mathematical engine underneath semantic search — not a linguistic operation at all, but a geometric one: given a target vector, find every stored vector close to it by some distance metric. A useful non-text analogy: imagine a room of people, each with an age and a height — Alice (25, 160cm), Bob (26, 162cm), Carol (45, 170cm), Dave (46, 172cm). Ask “find people similar to Alice” and a keyword match fails outright (no one else is named Alice), but plotting age against height and measuring distance immediately shows that Bob is close to Alice, while Carol and Dave — close to each other but far from Alice — are not similar to her. Vector databases do exactly this, just across hundreds of dimensions instead of two.
Concretely, this runs in three steps. First, embedding: both the query and every stored document are converted into vectors with the same embedding model — e.g., the query “happy dog” might embed as [0.9, 0.1, 0.8], a document “joyful puppy” as [0.88, 0.12, 0.79] (very close), and a document “sad cat” as [0.2, 0.9, 0.1] (far away). Second, distance calculation: pick a metric — cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, or dot product (see the table above) — and score every stored vector against the query vector. Third, nearest-neighbor search: find the top-k stored vectors with the highest similarity. A brute-force search compares the query against every single stored vector — accurate, but too slow once there are millions of them — so in practice vector databases use Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexing (HNSW, IVF) to find “good enough” neighbors in milliseconds instead.
For example, a user searching “steps to fix a flat tire” shows the gap directly:








Feature
Keyword search (old school)
Semantic / similarity search (modern)




How it searches
Scans literal strings of text characters
Converts the query to a vector; finds nearest-neighbor vectors


What it finds
Only documents containing the exact words “fix,” “flat,” and “tire”
Documents about “changing a punctured wheel” or “replacing a blown tire,” even without those exact words


Flaw
Misses relevant documents that use different vocabulary
Needs more compute and a purpose-built vector database




Summary







Concept
Explanation




Embedding
A list of numbers (vector) that captures the meaning of data


Vector database
A database optimized to search millions of embeddings by similarity, not exact match


Distance metric
A mathematical way to measure similarity (cosine, Euclidean, dot product)


Index (e.g., HNSW)
A pre-built structure that speeds up nearest-neighbor search dramatically


Use case
Powering LLM retrieval (RAG), semantic search, recommendations



The next lesson builds on all of this to cover chunking, the full RAG architecture, and the production patterns that turn a prototype retrieval demo into something reliable enough to ship. The lab notebook puts an HNSW-backed ChromaDB index, embeddings, and similarity search to work end to end.

title: Day 4 — Data Quality, Governance, and Lineage
text:
By Day 3 your pipelines move data — ingested, landed in bronze/silver/gold, served to a RAG index or a model. But moving data and moving trustworthy data are different problems. A pipeline can run green every single day, throw no exceptions, miss no SLA, and still be quietly wrong: a schema drifts, a source starts sending 25% nulls in a column nobody’s watching, a duplicate customer row skews a training set. Nothing crashes. The dashboard just starts lying, and the model just starts learning the wrong thing.
Today is about closing that gap. We look at the three pillars that turn a pipeline that merely runs into one that can be trusted, audited, and debugged:
None of these three work in isolation. A validation rule without governance has no owner to alert when it fires. A governance policy without lineage can’t tell you what a schema change will actually break. Together they turn raw, ungoverned data into an audited, secure, reliable asset — the same asset an AI system needs in order to be trusted with real decisions.

title: Automated Governance and Enterprise Policy
text: If data quality is about catching bad records, governance is about controlling who may touch data at all, and under what rules. Historically that meant a written policy document nobody re-read after onboarding. Increasingly, it means code: automated governance frameworks that enforce policy in real time as data moves through a pipeline, sitting underneath the human, legal enterprise governance policies that actually define what the rules are.
crumbs: Day 4 — Data Quality, Governance, and Lineage

title: Automated Governance and Enterprise Policy
section: From static rules to an automated control plane
text:
From static rules to an automated control plane
Automated data governance is the shift from static, written-down rules to dynamic, machine-learning-driven software that monitors, classifies, and protects data continuously as it flows. Done well, it is what lets an organization keep its data accurate, secure, consistent, compliant, and accessible without requiring heavy manual work — five properties a hand-maintained policy document could promise but rarely delivered at enterprise scale. Built on platforms like Collibra, Alation, Informatica CLAIRE, or open-source engines like Egeria, a modern framework operates as a control plane across four layers.





graph TD
    A["1. Automated Discovery & AI Classification"] --> B["2. Live Metadata Sync & Active Catalogs"]
    B --> C["3. Dynamic Policy & Real-Time Access Control"]
    C --> D["4. Automated Data Lineage — the paper trail"]







1. Automated discovery and AI classification
You cannot govern data you don’t know exists, and enterprises routinely have thousands of tables scattered across data lakes, cloud warehouses like Snowflake, and production databases. Machine learning models continuously scan storage environments, reading structural patterns, regex indicators, and value distributions instead of waiting for a human to label each column. The outcome: sensitive data — PII, credit-card numbers (PCI), medical data (HIPAA) — gets automatically flagged and tagged, with encryption or masking applied instantly.


2. Live metadata synchronization and active catalogs
Metadata — who owns a table, when it last changed, its schema — used to live in a hand-maintained data dictionary that was obsolete within weeks. Automated frameworks capture schema changes and update frequencies as they happen, building an always-accurate active catalog. If an engineer changes a column from an integer to a string, the catalog reflects that instantly, enterprise-wide.


3. Dynamic policy and real-time access control
Traditional security relies on static roles (“HR managers can see this table”). Modern frameworks shift to Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC), enforced directly inside the data pipeline: the system reads an asset’s metadata tag and cross-references it against compliance rules on the fly. If an analyst queries a table with customer history, the policy engine can mask just the social_security_number column while leaving the rest of the row available — security and usability at the same time.


4. Automated data lineage — the paper trail
When an executive looks at a dashboard number and asks “where did this come from, and can I trust it?”, lineage is the answer. Automated lineage differs from the legacy approach in every dimension that matters:








Feature
Legacy lineage
Automated lineage




Mapping method
Developers manually draw diagrams in Visio or map paths in spreadsheets.
A parsing engine reads SQL query history, dbt transformations, and orchestrator logs automatically.


Accuracy
Prone to human error and missing updates.
Accurate up to the second.


Impact analysis
Guessing what breaks if a schema changes.
Instant visual maps of every downstream dashboard or model that depends on a table.



We go deeper on the mechanics of lineage — including the concrete OpenLineage event format — in the next lesson.
In short: automated governance frameworks use automation and AI to manage quality, security, compliance, and monitoring across a modern data estate with far less manual overhead than the legacy, spreadsheet-driven approach.
crumbs: Day 4 — Data Quality, Governance, and Lineage

title: Automated Governance and Enterprise Policy
section: Enterprise governance policies — the human layer
text:
Enterprise governance policies — the human layer
If automated frameworks are the code enforcing rules in real time, enterprise governance policies are the actual laws, ethical guardrails, and corporate boundaries themselves — the strategic intent of the C-suite and legal department, defining how data must be handled, protected, and audited to survive in a regulated global economy. Enterprise governance policies more broadly are the formal rules covering how an organization manages operations, data, technology, security, employees, and compliance — ensuring the organization runs securely, efficiently, ethically, legally, and consistently.

The four cornerstones of enterprise governance policy
1. Regulatory compliance policies — the legal mandates. Non-negotiable rules dictated by governments; violating them risks massive fines, lawsuits, and executive liability.

Data sovereignty — data belonging to a country’s citizens must be physically stored and processed within that country’s borders (e.g. European data staying in the EU).
Regional mandates — GDPR (Europe, user deletion rights), CCPA/CPRA (California, consumer privacy), HIPAA (US) or MDR (Europe) for medical data.

2. Data privacy and access control policies — the security perimeter. Access follows the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP): an employee gets exactly the access their job requires, nothing more.

RBAC/ABAC — strict mandates on who can view what, e.g. “only HR directors with Level 3 clearance may view unmasked salary data.”
Classification schemes — every document or stream is labeled Public, Internal Only, Confidential, or Restricted.

3. Information Lifecycle Management (ILM) policies. Storing every byte forever is expensive, so ILM policies govern how data ages:








Policy phase
Corporate mandate
Action taken




Active retention
Keep hot, transactional data available for live reporting.
Stored in high-speed warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery) for up to 2 years.


Archival rules
Retain older, rarely-accessed but legally required data.
Moved to cold storage (e.g. AWS Glacier) for 7–10 years.


Defensible deletion
Destroy data once its legal retention window expires.
Automated hard-deletion and cryptographic shredding.



4. Responsible AI and generative AI governance policies. With LLMs and RAG systems now embedded in corporate workflows, companies have had to draft an entirely new policy layer: the “Shadow AI” blockade — employees are forbidden from pasting corporate code, proprietary designs, or customer PII into public consumer LLMs. A confidential spreadsheet uploaded to an external model to “make a quick chart” can be absorbed into that vendor’s training loop — a catastrophic, irreversible data breach.


Why this matters
Automated governance frameworks and enterprise governance policies are two halves of the same system: policy defines what is allowed, and the automated control plane makes that definition actually happen, continuously, without depending on every engineer remembering the rulebook. Neither one alone is sufficient — a policy with no enforcement is a suggestion, and enforcement code with no policy behind it has no legal or ethical grounding to enforce.

title: Day 5 — Architecture Integration and Final Project
text:
For four days you built the pieces one at a time: a lakehouse that stores data reliably (Day 1), a streaming layer that gets it there in real time (Day 2), a vector index and RAG pipeline that lets an AI system reason over it (Day 3), and a quality/governance/lineage layer that keeps the whole thing trustworthy and auditable (Day 4). Each of those days was deliberately self-contained — its own notebook, its own tools, its own narrow problem.
Today has no new tool to learn. Day 5 is where those four pieces stop being four separate labs and become one system. The technical question changes from “how does Kafka work” or “how does a vector index work” to “how do these things hand data to each other, in what order, and what happens when one of them fails or flags bad data.” That’s a systems-design question, not a new-library question — which is exactly the skill a production AI platform actually demands, and exactly what the capstone grades.
The practical skills the day is built around: combining all of this week’s components into one architecture, building a scalable AI data system out of them, presenting the architectural decisions behind that system, and simulating an enterprise production environment rather than a one-off notebook demo.
The second half of today is the final project: a single starter notebook that already runs end-to-end using lightweight stand-ins for every one of the week’s real tools, and your team’s job — in teams of three — is to replace those stand-ins with the real Kafka, Delta Lake, Great Expectations, and vector-DB code you already built earlier in the week.

Only install the extension dependencies for the specific real tools your team is integrating (Kafka, Delta Lake, Great Expectations, Airflow, etc.) — you don’t need all of them at once to get started. Open Day5_Lab.ipynb and run all cells top to bottom; the first code cell installs the starter’s own dependencies via !pip install.
Output lands in:

./lakehouse/silver/ — cleansed, validated records
./lakehouse/gold/ — revenue aggregation by country
./lineage_events/ — the pipeline’s JSON audit trail







Note



Module 4’s SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction downloads the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model from the Hugging Face Hub the first time it runs — this needs internet access on that first run (in Colab or locally); the model is cached afterward and subsequent runs are offline. On Windows, the Hugging Face cache also falls back to a non-symlinked copy of the model files instead of symlinks, which just uses a little more disk space — it does not affect correctness.
